en: *Rasārṇava-sudhākara*:
The *Rasārṇava-sudhākara* of Siṃhabhūpāla. Critically edited with introduction and notes by T. Venkatacharya. Madras:
Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1979.
The *Rasārṇavasudhākara* composed by the illustrious King Siṃha; First Vilāsa.
We worship that conjugal union which possesses the radiant joy of passion, the friendship of heroism, the fragrance of innocence and boldness,
and the nobility of both the Lāsya and Tāṇḍava dances.
I perpetually revere Sarasvatī, whose hand is marked by a lute, who has the eyes of a doe,
who is the goddess consisting of eternal bliss, and who is the beloved of the one seated upon a lotus.
There exists a certain supreme reality, the sprout of ultimate bliss, the space between the arms of one who is curious about the firmness of Kamalā’s breasts.
From his lotus feet was born a lineage free from all stain,
which attained the status of being a brother to the fruit of Bhagīratha’s ascetic penance.
There, the leader of the Dācaya clan was the lord Dācaya, a full moon in the autumn of the ocean of the Recarla lineage, a treasury of arts, and possessed of noble splendor.
Through the difficult path of his sword’s edge upon the battlefield,
the Goddess of Victory came from the elephant-host of the Pāṇḍya king.
In that Aṅganārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty was exceedingly firm,
the earth became a submissive female elephant under his control, serving as a goad for the rogue elephants that were wicked kings.
His wife was highly fortunate, renowned like Śrī herself;
she was Pōcamāmbā, noble in her virtues, born from a lineage as pure as the lotus.
To those two were born three sons, who were like wish-fulfilling trees for the earth and who terrified the heroic warriors of their enemies:
Siṃhaprabhu, Vennamanāyaka, and [the third].
The foremost of heroes and the lord of the earth, Reca.
In this Kali age, dharma, which consists of only a single quarter, has attained fullness through these very feet— as if they were its own steps— and thus no longer yearns for the Kṛta age.
While Siṃha was thus protecting the entire earth as its sovereign,
it was a marvel that the kings who bowed down experienced exaltation, while those who did not bow down experienced humiliation.
In the vicinity of Kṛṣṇeśvara, at Mel̥eśvara where great preparations had been made, that Lord— who,
by means of his various personal qualities, performed the installation of Brahman many times without any obstacle— attained freedom from debt.
In Brahmā, who is occupied with the weight of the effort involved in the excellence of his creative emanations.
Seeing his sword, which was as crooked as the tongue of Death, the enemies trembled; and from that,
a rise of sweat appeared in the minds of those who had gathered together.
It brings about the pacification of the heat of pride.
The illustrious Reca-Mahīpati, whose younger brother Su-carita clearly attained the far-reaching fame of being a preceptor to heroes and bore the insignia of a hero,
having acquired the title "Lord of the Kathāris" marked by the name Rāhuttarāya.
[He saw] his son, the leader of the Nāgas, the unique crest-jewel of heroes upon the earth.
This very Siṃhamahīpāla is clearly Vasudeva,
whose two sons, Ananta and Mādhava, are the protectors of the world.
There, his younger brother was Mādhava-nāyaka, whose majesty was renowned throughout the quarters of the world;
from him were born the kings who continued his lineage.
The preeminent mountain-kings of the Vedas became attenuated.
His elder brother, because he was not affected by the vices of kingship on earth, bore the name Anapota,
which was renowned and true to its meaning.
And he attained the perception of infinity and the state of being a mountain.
He whose brother is Balabhadra in form, whose beloved queen is Rukmiṇī, whose son is Pradyumna, and whose multitude of grandsons includes Aniruddha and others—
he is this very Lord of Lakṣmī, King Annapota; moreover, upon his lotus-like face—
And he bears the lovely beauty of the Sudarśana [discus] upon the lotus-hand of his own being.
Having made the earthly realm one where many sons of Soma protect it,
Hari feels ashamed while protecting the heavenly realm where only one son of Soma protects it.
While the one who is a Paraśurāma to the Soma clan,
terrifying in the strength of his arms, and a bull among men,
remains awake and rules there.
It eternally awakens the constant welfare of the worlds. //SRs_1.20//
Having placed a golden mountain within the reach of the gods on earth through his gifts of Hemādri,
he who constructed it with a path of beautiful stairways—
Śrīparvata, accessible to the feet of all people.
It is wondrous that he who is the destroyer of many heroes, though he is beyond numbering,
yet his own course and progression remain unbroken;
and though his existence is free from the confusion of birth, he is manifold.
It bears the mark of Bhārgava, who is of the lineage of Soma.
Running and running, enemy kings cast down upon the field of battle, beholding him before them with his body marked by sword-wounds at every stroke of the blade,
turned back from there and looked here and there for him whose—
They clearly and unerringly recognize him as bearing the marks of a Khadga and a Nārāyaṇa.
That lord of the earth had a queen renowned as Annamāmbā, who was as radiant as Śivā is to Śiva, the crest-jewel of kings. (SRs 1.24)
Śrutakīrti gladdens Śatrughna, and Subhadrā, dark-complexioned and radiant, gladdens her husband, the illustrious King Arjuna.
To those two were born two sons: the first was Veda-girīśvara, and the second was that peerless King Siṃha by virtue of his fame.
Then the illustrious King Siṃha, long-lived, shall unreservedly establish this earth firmly upon the seat of his own shoulders. (SRs 1.27)
With the bond of his bowstring unloosened, with a preeminent bow as radiant as gold, with arrows that destroy the enemy's strength, and with many hostile cities as his domain—
thus, for the most part, by means of this extraordinary method of preparation for battle, [he stands].
This is Maheśa, whom people call the lion-king.
And where there was the donning of armor for battle,
there was the treading of grass; and from one's own city,
there was the departure and the treading upon the forest.
Or attending upon those who are one's adversaries is a refuge for them. //SRs_1.29//
Bringing joy to the virtuous, causing the blue water-lilies to bloom,
nourishing the lovely arts, and even bearing the reputation of the physician Jīvātṛka—
oh, how this king intensely manifests the rising of his friend!
Likewise, [he experiences] the bliss of the *cakra*s as well as the exquisite splendor of the blossoming lotus.
Indeed, it is only when the drops of rain obtained from the dense clouds fall into oyster shells during the constellation Svāti that they attain the state of pearls in the ocean;
whereas those very droplets of water from their liberality, falling into the hands of the wise, become [pearls] immediately.
Rubies, magnificent garments, many dwellings, and gold.
Having recognized that this [king] possesses policy as his virtue and that his own position is devoid of virtue, the enemy kings—
[those who were once] experts in the virtues of policy— [sought refuge with him].
They bow down until they reach the seat of his lotus feet.
"Your subordinate kings have repeatedly sought refuge with me for the sake of preserving their lives; out of compassion, they ought to be protected by you"—
thus did his most intimate friends whisper into his ears, which were resting at the very edge of his hearing.
I believe that the wish-granting cow (Kāmadhenu) has taken refuge in the vicinity of the corners of his eyes.

When the enemies arrived, those women— who were experts in the art of repartee and the exchange of glances— spoke out of a sense of shame at the inquiries of the ladies of the inner apartments as to how they had protected their lives during the battle with Pragaṇḍabhairava.
The sprouts of the color of ruby-jewels shine from the swaying earrings on their ears.
Like the mandāra, pārijātaka, sandalwood, santāna, kalpavṛkṣa, and wish-fulfilling gem;
[he who is] the beloved of Anapota and Dācavallabha.
[The chapters] are designated as Veda, Giri, Svāmin, Māda, Dāma, and Ya.
He who shines upon this earth like a mine of jewels, possessing his own immense wealth and rejoicing in giving that which is not easily obtained by other people.
The exquisite splendor of his lotus-like feet was fashioned by the rays of the king's crown.

He whose first elder brother was the illustrious Annapota, a crest-jewel among princes distinguished by his virtues; who surpassed the elder brother of one [man] in personal beauty and wealth, the elder brother of two in archery,
and the elder brother of three when mounted on horseback— [that king] triumphs in the irresistible prowess of his arms.
In truthfulness he was like the four-faced Brahmā, and in generosity, moreover, like the five-faced Śiva.
In battle, the rival kings— tormented by the heat of his valor— plunge into the water of the edge of the blade of that Lord Kumāradāsa;
yet it is a marvel that his wives have their *tilaka* marks vanished and their dark curls disheveled.
The saffron from their breasts was falling away, and the black collyrium at the corners of their eyes was trickling down.
In whom, that cherished jewel of a son, the beloved full moon of King Vallabharāja,
the remaining power of the virtuous arises as it is nourished.
But the blossoming of lotuses is indeed wonderful. //SRs_1.39//
Together with these and other sons, this very Lion-King attains stability through six [members], like a master supported by well-united limbs.
That king occupied the capital named Rājācala, which had come down to him through the succession of his lineage;
therein he provided protection for the virtuous and instruction for the wicked.
Those who possess knowledge connect [the teachings] in accordance with logic. //SRs_1.41//
Protecting the circle of the earth between the Vindhya and Śrīśaila mountains with his sons who continue the lineage, this Indra among enjoyers partakes of all worldly objects.
While that son of Annapota, a delighter of the earth who was like a lion, ruled the land,

hardness resided in the circle of the breasts, tremulousness in the corners of the eyes of the fair-browed women; unevenness in the three folds of the waist, and faltering steps in their gait, which was languid with grace.
There is curliness in her tresses, and moreover, extreme slenderness is bound about her waist.
Therefore, for the sake of pleasing the learned, I shall set forth the definition of drama, which is the sole cause for the excellence of the color of that which possesses a beautiful form.
In ancient times, Purandara and the other gods, having bowed to the Four-faced One and joined their palms in reverence, questioned the All-knowing One.
O Blessed One, we wish to hear that which is worth hearing, beautiful to behold, captivating to the mind, righteous, conducive to fame, meaningful, and a demonstration of all arts. (SRs 1.46)
When they asked, "What is the fifth tradition that grants authority to all castes? Brahmā, recollecting all the Vedas, replied to them.
And having extracted the essence from those [Vedas], Prajāpati then created the Nāṭya-veda; after instructing the teacher Bharata, he spoke:
"Along with your sons, make this Veda manifest through its practical application.
Thus commanded by him, Bharata, together with his sons, [acted accordingly].
He performed [the dance] in the Sudharmā hall before Indra with hosts of apsarases,
and for the benefit of all the worlds, he composed the Nāṭyaśāstra.
Likewise, following that [tradition], Śāṇḍilya, Kohala, Dattila, Mataṅga, and others who were born from their lineages [composed works]. (SRs 1.51)

They composed various kinds of treatises and became renowned upon the earth; yet, because those works were exceedingly profound and their contents were scattered in a disordered sequence, [the tradition was difficult to grasp].
Due to the interruption of the tradition and the rarity of those who know it,
the path of dramaturgy has for the most part become obscure and its practice is infrequent.
Therefore, this effort of ours, characterized by the illumination of that [truth], delights the minds of the wise who grasp only the essence. (SRs 1.54)
Could a modern lamp not uproot the mass of darkness?
Does the moonlight, shining at that very time, not serve to satisfy the cakora birds?
And would the young sun not instantly cause the beds of lotuses to bloom?
Therefore, even now, these words of mine may indeed bring delight even to those such as I.
The path of drama, possessing a clear and sweet essence, enchanting with the shadows of its subject matter, and accompanied by its leading hero, is to be cultivated like a treasure of gold. (1.56)

Because, through enactments such as those characterized by the *sāttvika* [emotions] and others, the spectators develop a perception of identity with the protagonist in the actor, that is called *nāṭya*.
For the excellence of rasa is indeed the life-breath of drama;
therefore, it is defined by means of the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), the involuntary emotions (sāttvikas), and the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
The permanent emotion (sthāyībhāva), when brought to a state of sweetness, is known as rasa;
therein, the determinants (vibhāva) should be understood as the cause for making that rasa known.
This excitant (uddīpana) is to be known by the wise as being twofold—by way of its basis (ādhāra) and its object (viṣaya)—namely, the hero and the heroine. (SRs 1.60)
In this context, the object of focus is considered to be the virtuous Leader;
his qualities, moreover, are great fortune, magnanimity, steadfastness, and skill. (SRs 1.61)
Brilliance, righteousness, noble birth, eloquence, gratitude, knowledge of policy, purity, and possession of self-respect; SRs_1.62 //
Magnanimity, artistic skill, the quality of pleasing the subjects, and so forth—
these are declared by the wise to be the common virtues of a hero.
The state of sovereignty that surpasses all others is declared to be great fortune;
the wise know that the disposition to bestow such fortune is what constitutes magnanimity.
The wise say that steadfastness consists in carrying out an undertaking to its final result;
they describe dexterity as the ability to act swiftly in what is difficult.
The wise declare that brilliance is the quality of causing delight to the eyes;
being inclined toward righteousness is termed "virtuousness. (SRs 1.66)
Birth in a great family is declared by the wise to be noble lineage; eloquence, they say, is speech that is appropriate to the occasion. (SRs 1.67)
Gratitude is the recognition of benefits received;
skill in the means such as conciliation and the rest is declared to be knowledge of policy.
That purity which consists of the purification of the internal organ is proclaimed as *śucitā* (purity);
the state of possessing self-respect is said to be the quality of forbearance toward lack of miserliness.
Vitality is said to be the inability to endure contempt and the like;
possession of skill is declared to be proficiency in all branches of knowledge.
Captivatingness, moreover, consists in causing delight to the entire mind;
and a leader endowed with all the aforementioned qualities would be supreme.
The middling [hero] is one who lacks a few [qualities], while the one who lacks many qualities is called the inferior;
such is the fourfold leader: the *dhīrodātta* (noble and steadfast) and the *dhīralalita* (noble and playful).
Then he was known by the name Dhīrapraśānta, and later celebrated as Dhīroddhata;
he was compassionate, exceedingly profound, disciplined, and possessed of the essence of being.
Firm in his vows, patient, averse to self-praise,
and with his ego concealed— he is described by the wise as the *dhīrodātta* (the noble hero).
Compassion is defined as the state of possessing an excellence of mercy;
profundity is the absence of change even when a cause for agitation is present. (SRs 1.75)
Free from anxiety, steadfast yet graceful, youthful, and under the influence of women; by nature inclined toward tranquility, enduring of hardships, and discerning. (SRs 1.76)
Endowed with qualities such as gracefulness and the like, a Brahmin, a minister, or a merchant—
such as Cārudatta, Mādhava, and others— is cited as the *dhīra-śānta* (the calm and steadfast hero).
One who is possessive, egoistic, deceitful, irascible, fickle,
boastful— such as Bhārgava and others— is described as the *dhīroddhata* (the haughty hero).
And these leading characters are considered common to all aesthetic sentiments (rasas);
however, with respect to the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), their threefold classification is stated by the learned.
According to their distinctions, there are the husband (*pati*), the lover (*upapati*), and the paramour (*vaiśika*).
The husband is defined by the wise as the one who takes the hand according to the prescribed rite (*vidhi*).
That [hero] is also described as fourfold by those expert in poetry,
according to the distinction of being *anukūla* (favourable), *śaṭha* (deceitful), *dhṛṣṭa* (bold), or *dakṣiṇa* (cunning).
The *anukūla* (favourable) type is one who has only a single wife, yet is deceitful and commits offenses in secret;
he is audacious and remains fearless even when bearing the visible marks of enjoyment with other young women.
Among many heroines as well, one who behaves equally toward all is called *dakṣiṇa*;
he who, even without formal ritual, acts with a woman who has transgressed proper conduct.
He who is led by a sign and is so designated by the wise is called a *upapati*;
he possesses courtesy, compliance, and audacity due to his lack of fixed status.
Deceit is not appropriate for him, because of the possibility that his mind might be directed elsewhere;
he is handsome, endowed with virtue, learned in the scriptures, and pleasant to behold.
Of noble birth, intelligent, brave, endowed with pleasing attire, youthful,
undepressed, fragrant, generous, patient, and pleasant of speech.
Free from doubt and proud, he understands the distinctions of place and time,
and is endowed with dexterity, cleverness, sweetness, good fortune, and other such qualities.
One who is devoted to the enjoyment of courtesans is a *vaiśika*;
such characters as Kalakaṇṭha and others are to be recognized as *vaiśikas* specifically in the *bhāṇa* and similar genres.
It is described as being of three kinds, according to the distinction of superior, middling, and inferior;
furthermore, it consists of those who are suitable for providing assistance to the heroes of the erotic sentiment.
The *pīṭhamarda*, the *viṭa*, the *ceṭa*, and the *vidūṣaka* are defined as the hero’s attendants;
they are devoted to him and slightly inferior to him in his qualities.
One known as a *pīṭhamarda* is a conciliator of angry women; one who knows the arts of the *kāmatantra* is designated as a *viṭa*. (SRs 1.91)
The servant (ceṭa) is considered to be one such as Kalahaṃsa who is skilled in reconciling [quarrels];
the jester (vidūṣaka) causes laughter through his distorted limbs, speech, and dress.
Knowledge of place and time, sweetness of speech, elegance, skill in encouragement, and likewise speaking exactly as it has been said. //SRs_1.93//
"Secretiveness of counsel" and so forth are considered the qualities of assistants;
a heroine is considered one who is endowed with the qualities common to the leader. *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* 1.94.
She is of three kinds: one's own, another's, and common;
she is the one who does not abandon her beloved in times of prosperity or in times of adversity.
She who is endowed with the virtues of moral conduct and straightforwardness is called "one's own" by the wise;
and that "one's own" woman is said to be of three types: the innocent, the intermediate, and the mature.
The innocent girl, possessing the desire of fresh youth, is coy during lovemaking and tender in anger;
she exerts herself in amorous gestures while remaining subtly charming with her modesty.
When her beloved has committed an offense, she gazes at him while weeping;
she says nothing at all, whether it be unpleasant or even pleasant.
The *madhyā* heroine, whose modesty and passion are equal, endowed with burgeoning youth, desires her lover and is capable of amorous play that culminates in intense infatuation. (SRs 1.99)
The middling type of prideful behavior is threefold, consisting of the firm, the weak, and both; the firm woman, however, speaks to her offending lover with irony using indirect speech. (SRs 1.100)
The impatient woman vexes her beloved with harsh words in her anger; the woman who is both patient and impatient speaks to her lover with tears and indirect speech.
Intoxicated by the fullness of her youth, bold and with passion fully aroused,
she strives in the dalliances of love as if melting into the body of her beloved.
Even at the mere beginning of sexual union, she reaches a state of blissful intoxication;
though bold in her amorous conduct, she is further divided into three types according to the distinction of *dhīrā* (steadfast) and the others. 1.103.

In sexual union, the wise woman remains indifferent, while the one who is affected by affectation maintains a respectful air; however, the impatient woman, out of anger, will scold her lover harshly and even strike him.
Endowed with both steadfast and unsteadfast qualities, she is called "steadfast-unsteadfast" (dhīrādhīrā).
The "eldest" (jyeṣṭhā) and "youngest" (kaniṣṭhā) types are each twofold; the "middle" (madhyā) and "mature" (prauḍhā) types are likewise so.
The middling and mature women are each threefold according to the distinction between the steadfast, the unsteady, and so forth;
these are each further divided into two by the distinction between the elder and the younger. (SRs 1.106)
The *mugdhā* (the innocent girl) is of one kind, and thus she is said to be of thirteen types;
the other maiden (*kanyā*) is also of two kinds, distinguished as the unmarried girl and the married woman (*paroḍhā*).
In that context, the maiden (*kanyā*) is one who is unmarried, modest, protected by her father,
confident in the playful diversions of her female companions, and generally endowed with the qualities of an innocent girl (*mugdhā*).
This [type of heroine] may be either primary or secondary in dramas and the like;
in the *Mālatīmādhava*, for example, Mālatī and Madayantikā serve as such.
But a woman who, though married by another, is longing for the enjoyment of another man, is to be identified as the *paroḍhā* in minor compositions such as the *Saptaśatī* by the wise. (SRs 1.110)
A common woman is a courtesan endowed with artistic skill, proficiency, and boldness;
she is of two kinds, distinguished by whether she is attached or detached. (SRs 1.111)
In that regard, the *raktā* (attached) heroine should be described as being of secondary importance in a drama, such as Queen Irāvatī in the case of King Agnimitra. (SRs 1.112)
Whether primary or secondary, she [the heroine] appears in dramatic forms other than the *nāṭaka*;
however, in the *nāṭaka*, if she is divine, she is described as being primarily so.
The dispassionate woman, however, is described as engaging in jesting and the like; her fortitude and other such qualities are conducive to that state. (SRs 1.114)
She should inflame with passion the wealthy fools and heretics who conceal their desires and seek only carnal pleasure; she should banish the penniless by means of small measures.
On this point, some say:
"A courtesan has no affection even for a hero endowed with virtues;
and if she were described as being without passion, it would result in the fault of a mere semblance of rasa."
And for this reason, she should not be the subject of description in dramas and the like;
thus they have said: "A courtesan is a common woman; she is to be sought by one who desires wealth above all else. (Śṛṅgāratilaka 1.62, 64)
"There is neither aversion toward one devoid of qualities nor affection toward one possessed of qualities;
in these women, there is only a semblance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārābhāsa), never the erotic sentiment itself."
The wise King Śrī Siṃha does not approve of that opinion.

Furthermore, because the absence of the persistence of her emotional state would contradict her status as a heroine, and because her status as a heroine is established by the context and other such factors at the beginning of the work. (SRs 1.117)

But in the description of a heroine who is not the central figure, there arises the contingency of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa); likewise, because the context and other factors result in the absence of a substratum for rasa.

However, because it contradicts such scriptural authorities as the statement that "the substratum of rasa is tenfold," [it follows that] in the case of common women, when the hero is endowed with excellent qualities... [SRs 1.119]
The connection with the emotional state (*bhāva*) would indeed exist, according to the statement of Rudraṭa as well;
some even consider this to apply to all varieties, such as the *udātta* and others. (SRs 1.120)
These [types of women] are generally seen everywhere in common usage;
first is the one whose husband has gone abroad (*proṣitapatikā*), then the one adorned for her lover (*vāsakasajjā*), and thereafter the one longing in separation (*virahotka*).

Now, she who is considered "the neglected" (*khaṇḍitā*), as well as "her who has been separated by a quarrel" (*kalahāntaritā*), "the woman going to meet her lover" (*abhisārikā*), "the deceived" (*vipralabdhā*), "he whose husband is under his own control" (*svādhīnapati*), and another [type] have been described. (1.122)
These [heroines] are divided into eight types according to the different stages produced by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
When her beloved has gone to a distant land, she becomes a woman whose husband is away (*proṣitabhartṛkā*).
Her symptoms, however, are wakefulness, emaciation, gazing at various signs and omens, soiling herself, restlessness, and generally remaining upon her bed. (SRs 1.124)
States such as dullness and anxiety are described by the wise as "transformations" (vikriyā);
Bharata and others, however, have declared the "turning" (vāra) to be the occasion for women's rendezvous.
She who, out of regard for her own lover, prepares herself within the house when he is about to arrive at his beloved's home, is called *vāsakasajjikā*. (SRs 1.126)
Her activities, however, consist of brooding over the desire for union,
diversion with her friends, writing love-letters to her heart's beloved, and repeatedly watching for the female messenger.
Those [states] beginning with gazing at the path by which her beloved approaches are considered [the characteristics of the *utkaṇṭhitā*];
she who is anxious because her most beloved lover is delayed despite being innocent.
She who is distressed by the longing of separation has been described by those who understand emotional states;
her symptoms, however, are a burning in the heart, trembling, and a failing of the limbs.
Discontent, shedding tears, recounting her own condition, and so forth—these occur when her beloved, having transgressed the agreement, enjoys another woman. (SRs 1.130)
Adorned with the marks of enjoyment, she who arrives in the morning is indeed the *khaṇḍitā* (the neglected wife);
her thoughts, sighs, silence, and shedding of tears are her [expressions of grief]. (SRs 1.131)

Exhaustion, confusion, indistinct speech, and so forth are considered the physical manifestations [of anger], when one, out of wrath, [acts] toward a beloved who has fallen at her feet in the presence of her friends. (SRs 1.132)
For it is she who, having cast him aside, later suffers from being separated by quarrels;
but in her case, delusion is her wandering speech, and her sighing is her fever.

Frequent lamentation and other such actions performed by one tormented by the fire of passion, through which she causes her beloved to come to her, are designated as "longing" (iṣṭā) by the wise. (SRs 1.134)
She who goes out at night, adorned with garments and ornaments suitable for travel under the moonlight,
or who goes out of her own accord, is an *abhisārikā*.
Her transformations, such as distress and anxiety, are appropriate for her own secret meeting with her lover, arising from the apprehension that she might lose her modesty and so forth.
Her eyes were like those of a fawn terrified by the roar of a tiger,
and her body was veiled in a garment dyed with indigo and other colors.
With her limbs dissolved into her own body, moving silently on foot,
she proceeds full of longing, accompanied only by one very affectionate female companion.
While her lover slept feigning sleep, she remained motionless at his side,
restrained by an excess of pride, though cooled by garlands, sandalwood paste, and other fragrant unguents.
Understanding his state of mind and eager to observe his condition, she awakens him;
she is to be known as one's own maiden in the process of approaching her beloved. (SRs 1.140)
But the courtesan, going to meet her lover, approaches him joyful, with a face manifesting a smile and eyes rolling with intoxication. (SRs 1.141)
With her entire body anointed and adorned with various ornaments,
the god of love became manifest through the horripilation sprouting from her affection.
She was surrounded by her attendants, who were provided with all the requisites for enjoyment;
the power of the god of love was awakened by the sweetness of the tinkling of their waist-bands.
And she is beautiful with the jeweled anklets clinging to her lotus-feet, and [she delights me] with soft touches such as scratching my hair. (SRs 1.144)
When he awakens, she rouses him out of affection with eyes full of anger,
her jasmine flowers in her disheveled hair falling as they are tossed by the movement of her arms.
Her eyes were made lovely by the playfulness of moving eyebrows and other such gestures;
her speech was faltering with the intoxication of incessantly tasting liquor.
Proudly accompanied by her maidservants,
she approaches her beloved with the ringing of her bracelets and the gentle fanning of a fan.
She who, having made an appointment, becomes distressed when her lover does not arrive due to fate, awakens him and rebukes him with the breaking of her nose.
The wise have declared that this [state] is called *vipralabdha* (deception); its manifestations include despondency, anxiety, exhaustion, tears, fainting, sighing, and so forth.
With her husband nearby and under her own control, she is joyful, for her beloved is subject to her will;
her activities are said to be a great festival of worship for the God of Love.
Sports in the forest, water-play, gathering flowers, and so forth—thus all women are of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (SRs 1.151)
She who is desired by those of noble birth, those satisfied with worldly enjoyments, and those possessed of virtue,
displays anger for a cause and becomes gracious when conciliated.
She who does what is unpleasant for her husband while herself performing what is pleasing,
and who remains silent even when her beloved has committed an offense— she is the most excellent woman.
A woman who desires a man on her own, or is desired by him as a bride;
who becomes angry repeatedly when he is angry, and speaks falsehood when he is untruthful—[she is a *vadhū*]. (SRs 1.154)
She who returns harm for harm, yet feels affection for her beloved when he is kind—
endowed with such qualities as these, she is proclaimed to be the "mediocre" (madhyamā) woman.
She becomes angry without cause and does not relinquish her resentment even when entreated; she cares neither for beauty nor ugliness, nor for virtue nor its absence. (SRs 1.156)
Whether it be an elder or even a youth, she who repeatedly desires him and remains constant amidst jealousy, anger, and quarrels is known as the *sādharmā*.
The woman belonging to oneself (*svīyā*) is of thirteen types, and the courtesan (*vaiśikā*) is of various kinds;
thus, there are sixteen types in total, categorized according to eight stages.
Each one of these [three hundred] is divided eightfold according to the distinctions of "superior" and so forth;
thus, there are three hundred and eighty-four varieties.

Some say that there are only three states of a man's paramour: the female messenger (dūtī), the female friend (sakhī), and the female servant (ceṭī); [furthermore,] the female ascetic (liṅginī) and the neighbor (prativeśinī). (SRs 1.160)
The nurse’s daughter, the artisan, the young girl, the spinner,
the female laborer, and the female fortune-teller— these are endowed with the qualities of a leader and a friend.

The excitant (uddīpana) is fourfold, distinguished as: the objective basis (ālambana), the substratum (samāśraya), qualities (guṇa), actions (ceṣṭā), and ornaments (alaṅkṛti), as well as those that are extrinsic (taṭastha). SRs 1.162.
Youth, beauty and charm, loveliness, handsomeness,
gentleness, and delicacy— these are the qualities pertaining to the objective support.
The youth of all women is indeed fourfold;
for each stage of youth, their behaviors are distinct.
With the corners of her eyes slightly tremulous, her lotus-face smiling with passion,
her cheeks flushed with the bloom of pride, and her lower lip not yet fully crimson.
Her limbs are beautiful with the blossoming of loveliness, fragrant with the scent of radiant emotion;
her breasts have put forth budding sprouts, yet the joints of her body remain indistinct.
In her first youth, that fawn-eyed woman desires gentle touch and cannot endure passionate lovemaking.
Delighting in play with her friends and attentive to the adornment of her own limbs,
she does not experience anger or joy upon seeing her co-wife and the like.
She does not become excessively impassioned in the company of her beloved, but rather feels bashful;
her breasts are full, her waist is slender, and there is a reddish glow in her hands and feet.
Her thighs were shaped like the trunks of elephants, her limbs possessed clearly defined joints,
her hips were broad, her navel was deep, and her loins were firm.
The line of hair was clearly visible, and there was luster in her limbs, hair, and eyes;
thus, that lovely-eyed woman was endowed with a second youth.
Generally, a proud woman who knows the intentions of her friends remains affectionate toward them,
yet she does not yield to conciliation and is envious of her co-wives.
Turbid with the jealousy born of her affection, she cannot endure offenses;
proud in private, she acts without restraint during amorous dalliances.
There is a lack of moisture in the eyes, a fading of luster on the cheeks, a loss of radiance,
a roughness to the touch, and even a slight flaccidity of the limbs.
In the third stage of youth, the passion on the lower lip becomes smooth;
therein lies this behavior of women: their proficiency in the art of lovemaking.
Not abandoning her beloved, skill in attracting him, disregard for his offenses, and freedom from envy even toward his other wives. (SRs 1.176)
In the fourth stage of youth, a woman experiences a withered state and a loss of flesh in her breasts, hips, cheeks, thighs, loins, and other parts. (SRs 1.177)
In that regard, her physical gestures consist of a lack of enthusiasm for sexual union, a sense of incapacity,
compliance toward co-wives, and remaining in a state of non-separation from her beloved.
In that regard, the suitability for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the cause of aesthetic delight,
exists only in the first and second [types of *śleṣa*], and not in the third and fourth.
When the limbs, though not yet adorned with ornaments such as earrings and the like,
appear as if they were already adorned by that [intrinsic quality], it is called *rūpa* (beauty).
That which appears within the limbs like the shimmering quality of a shadow within pearls is here called *lāvaṇya*.
That arrangement of the major and minor limbs which is appropriate and characterized by well-knit joints and bonds is called beauty (saundarya). (SRs 1.182)
When, by means of the excellence of its own qualities, one brings another nearby object into a state of similarity, that is called *ābhirūpya* (beauty) by the wise. (SRs 1.183)
That part of the body which, when touched, feels as if it were untouched is indeed *mārdava* (softness);
it is the inability of even a delicate object to endure contact upon the limbs. (SRs 1.184)
That delicacy is of three kinds according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior:
that by which a limb cannot endure the touch of flowers and the like is the superior [delicacy]. (SRs 1.185)
That limb which cannot endure even the touch of the hand is indeed middling; that limb which cannot endure heat and so forth is here considered inferior.
The fourfold ornamentation consists of clothing, jewelry, garlands, and unguents;
there are also those that are peripheral, such as moonlight, a fountain-house, and the rising of the moon.
The *kokila* birds warble, gentle breezes blow from the mango groves, bees hum, and the arbors of creepers, the ground-houses, and the ponds provide cooling water. (SRs 1.188)
Palaces, inner chambers, music, play, mountains, rivers, and so forth—
these should be understood accordingly as being useful for enjoyment at the appropriate times.
Those gestures and manifestations directed toward an object,
which directly reveal the state of mind residing within one's own cause,
are known as *anubhāvas*, such as the raising of the eyebrows, smiles, and so forth. (SRs 1.190)
These arise from fourfold undertakings of mind, body, speech, and intellect;
therein are *bhāva*, *hāva*, *helā*, *śobhā*, *kānti*, and *dīpti*.
Boldness, sweetness, fortitude, and magnanimity are states born of the mind;
the state of a mind that is free from modification would be the first modification [of the self]. (SRs 1.192)
That slight manifestation of feeling which, joined with the movement of the neck and the play of the eyebrows, eyes, and so forth, is called *hāva*. (SRs 1.193)

*Hela* is indeed *hāva* itself, made manifest through various transformations that indicate the form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and consisting of graceful gestures (*lalitābhinaya*). (SRs 1.194)

That splendor which arises from beauty, enjoyments, and so forth, and which serves as an adornment of the limbs, is called *kānti* (loveliness); it is radiant and nourishes the god of love. (SRs 1.195)
Beauty itself [is enhanced] by factors such as age, enjoyment, place, time, and quality.
If the radiance has reached an excessively expanded state due to being ignited, it is called *dīpti* (radiance).
Freedom from hesitation in one's actions is proclaimed as boldness (*prāgalbhya*);
and what is called sweetness (*mādhurya*) is gentleness in all states of physical movement.

That which is a steady elevation of the mind is designated as "fortitude" (dhairya); the wise declare that "magnanimity" (audārya) is a state of discipline that persists through all conditions. (SRs 1.198)
Līlā, vilāsa, vicchitti, vibhrama, kilakiñcita,
moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭamita, bibboka, and likewise lalita.
And "the playful movement" (vihṛta) is to be known as the tenth among the bodily gestures of women;
it consists of imitating one's beloved, preceded by sweet speech.
That [expression] which occurs through gestures or movements of the eyebrows, eyes, and face at the moment of attaining a beloved is called *līlā*. (SRs 1.201)
That particularity which is momentary is called *vilāsa* (graceful play); even a slight arrangement of ornaments produces an exceeding beauty.

At the time of going to meet her beloved, due to the agitation caused by the onset of passion, there occurs a confusion consisting of the displacement of ornaments such as armlets and necklaces from their proper places. (SRs 1.203)
The mingling of grief, anger, tears, joy, and so forth, characterized by a "something-or-other" (kila-kiñcitam) that reveals one's own desire, is called *moṭṭāyita*. (SRs 1.204)
When the mind rejoices at the seizing of the hair, the lower lip, and so forth,
yet she acts as if distressed externally and becomes angry, that is indeed *kuṭṭamita*.
Disregard even toward a beloved due to pride or vanity is called *bibboka*; it consists of graceful postures and gestures of the limbs, made charming by the playfulness of the eyebrows. (SRs 1.206)
Where there is delicacy, that is called *lalita* (the playful);
when, due to jealousy, pride, or shame, a fitting reply is not given. (SRs 1.207)
"That which is manifested through action is called *vihṛtam* (the playful); thus was it declared by the illustrious King Siṃha, who was adorned with the ornament of goodness. (SRs 1.208)
Thus, twenty ornaments of women born of their inner nature (*sattva*) have been described;
from that same *sattva* arise only the ten states (*bhāva*) and so forth, but not the playful gestures (*līlā*) and the rest.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to say that there are twenty *sāttvika* states;
rather, the quality of being *sāttvika* is logically applicable only to those things that accompany the [eight] primary *bhāvas* and so forth.
By the force of the "umbrella" maxim (*chatrinyāya*), even the ten-fold group beginning with *līlā* is clearly understood;
thus, *krīḍita* and *kelī* are recorded by Bhoja as two further varieties arising from the body (*gātraja*).
Therefore, in this case of "twenty," the object to be numbered is not logically established; to this, King Siṃha, who knows the reality of existence, replies: [SRs 1.212]

The first [type of hero] is not considered among the [eight] experiences (anubhāvas), because even before the emergence of passion and so forth, during his childhood, he was merely engaged in the diversions of a maiden.
Because they consist solely of love and confidence, they do not possess the status of being "consequents" (anubhāvas) for anything else;
therefore, this number of twenty is accepted by those who know how to count.
Beauty, gracefulness, sweetness, fortitude, profundity, as well as charm, magnanimity, and splendor—these are the varieties of *sattva* belonging to men. (SRs 1.215)
Where compassion, rivalry, heroism, enthusiasm,
and skill manifest in abundance, that is proclaimed as *śobhā* (splendor).
A gait as deep as that of a bull, a steady gaze,
and speech accompanied by a smile— where these are present, it is called *vilāsa* (grace).
That sweetness (*mādhurya*) consists in the desirability of one's gestures, glances, and so forth;
where gestures abound with erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra*), that is *lalita* (the graceful). (SRs 1.218)
In this context, profundity and fortitude are born of the mind, while the others are born of the body; some authorities consider these to be common to both mind and body. (SRs 1.219)
Speech, lamentation, conversation, idle chatter, repetitive talk, denial, a message, and an extension [of a rule]. //SRs_1.220//
Exposition, instruction, indirect indication, and designation—thus have the twelve types of verbal expression been proclaimed and celebrated by the wise. (SRs 1.221)
In this context, *ālāpa* is pleasant speech, while *vilāpa* is speech born of sorrow;
a discourse consisting of question and answer is celebrated as *saṃlāpa*. (SRs 1.222)
Meaningless talk is *pralāpa*; repeated speech is *anulāpa*; whereas *apalāpa* is the misrepresentation of what was previously stated. (SRs 1.223)

A *sandeśa* (message) is the sending of news concerning one who is away; it is an *atideśa* (extended application), which consists of speech such as "these words were spoken by me" or "those words were spoken by him. (SRs 1.224)
This very discourse, such as "I am this" and so forth, would be the exposition (*nirdeśa*);
where there is speech for the purpose of training, that is called instruction (*upadeśa*). (SRs 1.225)
Where there is the mention of one thing for the sake of another, that is called *apadeśa*;
where one's own desire is expressed under a pretext, this is termed *vyapadeśaka*. (SRs 1.226)
Thus, the undertakings of the intellect are said to be *rīti*, *vṛtti*, and *pravṛtti*.
*Rīti* is the artful arrangement of words, and it is considered to be of three kinds. (SRs 1.227)
It may be soft, hard, or mixed; therein, the soft [vṛtti] is that which is composed of few consonants from the second and fourth classes. (SRs 1.228)
It consists mostly of syllables with few vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is endowed with ten vital breaths, is devoid of compounds, or is adorned with very few compounds. (SRs 1.229)
Because it is pleasing to the people of Vidarbha, that style is called Vaidarbhī. [Its qualities are:
cohesion (śleṣa), clarity (prasāda), evenness (samatā), sweetness (mādhurya), and delicacy (sukumāratā).
Clarity of meaning, loftiness, vigor, grace, and meditative concentration—these ten qualities are remembered as the very life-breath of the Vaidarbha style. (SRs 1.231)
That in which looseness—characterized by a mere paucity of breaths, phonemes, words, and their arrangement—is not touched upon, is declared to be *śleṣa* (cohesion). //SRs_1.232//
That which consists of words with well-known meanings is called *prasāda* (clarity); the absence of unevenness in the composition of words is *samatā* (evenness). (SRs 1.233)
Binding is said to be of three kinds: soft, clear, and mixed.
That sweetness (*mādhurya*) exists where the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is manifest in both word and meaning. (SRs 1.234)
That which consists of non-harsh phonemes is called *saukumārya* (softness), whereby a sentence being heard does not provoke a desire for other words. (SRs 1.235)
That which conveys the meaning is considered this very "clarity of meaning" (*arthavyakti*);
when a sentence is uttered, the manifestation of excellence in its qualities is "loftiness" (*udāratā*). (SRs 1.236)
The abundance of compounds is proclaimed as *ojas* (vigorousness), which is the presentation of charming meanings without transgressing the conventions of the world. (SRs 1.237)
Luster (kānti) is known to be twofold: in narrative accounts and in descriptions.
Samādhi is the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another. (SR 1.238)

That which is joined with excessively long compounds, abounding in many syllables and aspirated sounds, is called the Gauḍīyā style because it is pleasing to the minds of the scholars of that region. (SRs 1.239)
Where the collection of both sets of qualities is balanced like a scale, that is the *miśrā* (mixed) style; it is called *pāñcālī*, and it is favored by those born in that region.
The Āndhrī, Lāṭī, Saurāṣṭrī, and other such mixed styles exist, distinguished by the particular combinations favored by the learned of their respective regions. (SRs 1.241)
Those very same words and combinations of words, those very same manifestations of meaning—
nevertheless, poetry becomes new through the skill of its composition.
I shall not state their definitions here, as they are merely verbose and cumbersome;
those who desire them should look for them in the compositions of Bhoja and others.
Bhāratī, Sātvatī, Kaiśikī, and Ārabhaṭī—these are the four styles (vṛtti); their origin will be clearly explained.
When the world had become a single ocean, the imperishable Lord, the Supreme Person,
reclining upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa, became absorbed in yogic sleep.
Then the two lords of the Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, intoxicated by the pride of their prowess, approached the Lord of the God of Gods with speed, desiring battle.
Uttering various harsh words and insults,
the two of them fought Hari with blows from their fists and knees.
The Lord of Creatures, born from the lotus at his navel, spoke:
"Why does this activity of Bharatī still continue even now? (SRs 1.248)
"Therefore, O Lord, lead these two invincible ones swiftly to their destruction.
Having heard these words of his, Janārdana replied:
This speech was surely fashioned for the purpose of composing poetry; because of its eloquence and abundance of expression, it shall be known as Bhāratīya.
Having spoken these words, "I shall slay these two this very moment," Hari [addressed them] with pure, unchanging, and enchanting words accompanied by gestures and ornaments.
With his limbs, he fought those two Daitya lords who were skilled in combat,
employing various ground-based stances and the placement of Hari’s feet.
Then the earth became a burden because of that;
yet, by his power, it was [lightened] there by the radiant leaps of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, which were free from agitation.
Then Hari, with his powerful arms preeminent in strength, effortlessly displayed the conduct of a Sātvata through various graceful movements of his limbs.
Because he seized them by the hair, that [style] originated as Kaiśikī;
it is characterized by impetuosity, speed, and the execution of various wonderful movements (cārīs).
From that, the *ārabhaṭī* style arose through various wrestling maneuvers,
because the crushing of the Dānavas was accomplished by means of diverse *aṅgahāras*.
Therefore, the Lord born from the lotus established the rules for wrestling in this world;
whatever is the proper method regarding the discharge of weapons and missiles has been prescribed therein.

In the application of dramatic and poetic composition, that very same *samaya* (convention), which rests upon aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotional state (*bhāva*), has been designated by the Creator as "vṛtti" (mode).
Just as that object was made by Hari with such arching gestures,
even so was her bodily form fashioned by the Creator in that very same manner.
Others, however, declare that Bhāratī and the others were born in sequence from the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda respectively. (SRs 1.260)
Because it is employed by the descendants of Bharata, it is called Bhāratī;
since it is useful for the prologue (prastāvanā), it is defined there along with its constituent parts.
She who is endowed with the quality of *sattva*—such as extreme generosity, heroism, and so forth—and who is characterized primarily by joy while having abandoned all states of grief; //SRs_1.262//
That mode of performance is called Sātvatī by those learned in its characteristics; it has four components: Saṃlāpa (dialogue) and Uttāpa (distress), as well as [the others].
The characteristics of the *saṅghātya* and the *parivarta* are now stated:
[they are composed] with states such as envy and anger, and with aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) such as the heroic and the marvelous.
A conversation consisting of profound speech between one another is called *saṃlāpa*; that which, at the outset, incites another toward battle is known as *utthāpaka*.
Whether by the power of mantras, by the power of wealth, by the power of fate, or through human effort,
that which causes a schism in the Saṅgha is declared to be *saṅghātya*.
The abandonment of a task previously undertaken in order to take up another task is to be known as *parivartaka* (exchange). // SRs 1.267 //
The Kaiśikī style is characterized by soft amorous gestures such as dancing, singing, and playful dalliance, and it is adorned with delicate ornaments.
Its limbs are four, preceded by *narma* (jesting);
*sphañja*, *sphoṭa*, and *garbha*—their definitions are now stated.
Parihāsa (jesting) is that which abounds in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), delights the heart of the beloved, and is free from vulgarity; it is considered to be of three kinds. (SRs 1.270)
The *narma* (jest) arising from the erotic and the comic, that arising from the pure comic, and that arising from fear and the comic—this threefold *narma* has been proclaimed. (SRs 1.271)
Through the manifestation of a desire for enjoyment, through the instillation of passion,
and likewise through the disclosure of a beloved who has committed an offense.
The manifestation of the desire for enjoyment is threefold, through speech, dress, and gestures;
likewise, the display of passion is threefold, like playful dalliance born of the desire for enjoyment.
The disclosure of a lover’s transgression is likewise said by the wise to be of three kinds;
similarly, that which arises from pure laughter is also said by the wise to be of three kinds. (1.274)

That which arises from laughter produced by fear is called "fear-and-laughter-born" (*bhayahāsyaja*); it is of two kinds. However, both that [laughter] and the [fear] have three varieties each, as previously stated. (SRs 1.275)
By King Siṃha, who understood the creation of refined and non-vulgar humor,
the eighteenfold division of *narma* (jesting) was clearly illustrated.
In a new union, there is a "burst of play" (*narma-sphañja*) characterized by easy effort and ending in fear;
however, a "burst of play" (*narma-sphoṭa*) indicated by the various emotional states (*bhāva*) would possess little rasa.
Others, however, describe "interruption of enjoyment at an inappropriate time" as an action undertaken by either the hero or the heroine for the sake of achieving their own ends. (SRs 1.278)
But that which is intent on concealment and contains a jest is called *narma-garbha*;
it is where the hero who was previously situated perishes and another takes his place.
For Bharata, the master of the Nāṭya-veda, declares that this [drama] also contains elements of humor,
as well as a wealth of illusory magic, conjurations, and various modes of combat.
They know the *ārabhaṭī* style to be composed of actions involving cutting, piercing, and leaping;
its four constituent parts (*aṅga*) are *saṅkṣipti*, *avapātana*, [ *vikṣepa*, and *sampheta* ]. (SR 1.281)
Those who came before have declared that *vastūtthāpana* and *sampheṭa* are those [types of drama] which, though employing illusion and artifice, have a concise subject matter and plot. (SRs 1.282)
That is called *saṅkṣipti* by the high-souled Bharata;
others, however, describe it as the connection with another state of the protagonist. (1.283)
Because it involves the distinction of shifting [the subject], we shall disregard that;
for there would be confusion and a downfall through entering, running, and fleeing.
The provocation of that object refers to an object imagined through illusion;
whereas *sampheṭa* (clashing) is the mutual encounter of two people who are enraged and agitated.
And among these modes [of expression], the *śabdavṛtti* (verbal mode) is *bhāratī*;
the remaining three are *arthavṛttis* (modes of meaning), for those are indeed the four modes.

Others, however, maintain that through the blending of these [styles], there is a fifth style, the mixed (miśrā), which possesses the common characteristics of all rasas without exception; they thus define it. (SRs 1.287)

The Kaiśikī style is appropriate for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), while the Sāttvatī is for the heroic (vīra). The Ārabhaṭī style, moreover, is fixed for the furious (raudra) and the loathsome (bībhatsa).
The Bhāratī style is indeed desired in all the sentiments (rasas), beginning with the erotic;
however, some regard this verse as a restrictive rule specifically for the Bhāratī.
The wise, explaining [the matter] with the intention that it is generally the case,
do not accept a fixed rule for these functions regarding the sentiments (rasas).
"We remain indifferent toward this path, for it would not be beautiful when subjected to critical inquiry;
[so too is] the conceptualization of the *kaiśikī* style and its various divisions, such as *narma* (jesting) and the like. (SRs 1.291)
That which, by relying on compassion, serves as the cause for the semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) will be clearly explained here in this section on the semblance of rasa. SRs 1.292.
The fourfold commentary has been clearly demonstrated by King Siṃha, who is proficient in those respective methods and follows the path of logic.
The language, actions, dress, and customs appropriate to each respective region—therein, language is divided into two types: *bhāṣā* and *vibhāṣā*. (SRs 1.294)
In that regard, there are seven kinds of speech: Prācyā, Āvantyā, Māgadhī, Bāhlīkā, Dākṣiṇātyā, Śaurasenī, and Mālavī. (SRs 1.295)
There are seven types of Prakrit, beginning with Vibhāṣā: those born of the Śabaras, Dramiḷas, and Āndhras;
and those arising from the Śakas, Ābhīras, Caṇḍālas, and forest-dwellers.
There are other languages and dialects appropriate for the people of various regions;
however, because they are of no utility here, their characteristics are not described. (SRs 1.297)

The dress appropriate to each respective region and the activities with their very distinct differences, as well as the cultivation of [compassion] toward the states of pleasure, pain, and so forth experienced by others; SRs 1.298.
That state of mind which proceeds in accordance with the aspirations of practitioners should be understood as "sattva" by the wise, for these [qualities] arise from sattva. (SRs 1.299)
The great seers, such as Bharata and others, know them as *sāttvika*, for by means of them the true nature (*sva-sattva*) of all emotional states (*bhāva*) is indeed manifested. (SRs 1.300)
Those states have been declared as *sāttvika* by those who know the reality of the *bhāvas*:
they are paralysis, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, and trembling. (SRs 1.301)
Change of color, and the shedding of tears—these eight are proclaimed;
while paralysis arises from joy, fear, indignation, despondency, and wonder. (SRs 1.302)
These are the manifestations of the pillar (stambha) recognized by the sages:
the state of being devoid of perception, emptiness, and immovability.
Sweat is produced there due to heat, joy, physical exertion, fatigue, anger, fear, and so forth; these, however, are its external manifestations (anubhāvas).
The desire for the removal of perspiration and wind, the taking up of a fan, and so forth;
the bristling of the hair caused by wonder, enthusiasm, joy, and the like—these are the physical transformations in that state. (SRs 1.305)
The touch of limbs covered in bristling hair, a change in voice, and such as stammering may occur there due to pleasure, pain, and other emotions. (SRs 1.306)
Trembling may arise from joy, terror, old age, anger, and so forth;
in that context, its consequent expressions (anubhāvas) are considered to be throbbing, shaking of the limbs, and the like.
Discoloration arises from grief, heat, anger, and the like;
the transformations therein include the alteration of facial complexion, emaciation, and so forth.
Tears arise from despondency, anger, or joy;
their actions include the shedding of teardrops and the wiping of the eyes. (SRs 1.309)
Dissolution consists of suffering, destruction, and so forth; therein lies the state of unconsciousness.
Although all phenomena are indeed composed of *sattva* because they are rooted in *sattva*, [they are characterized by these states]. (SRs 1.310)
Nevertheless, because these have their sole root in *sattva*, they are designated as *sāttvika*;
and these are called *anubhāvas* (consequents) because they indicate the *bhāvas* (transitory emotions). (1.311)
Thus has their twofold nature been described by those skilled in the theory of aesthetic emotion (bhāva):

by the illustrious King Siṃha, who was a unique treasury of aesthetic power and possessed of the experience of bliss, the various states of aesthetic power (anubhāvas) have been defined along with their constituent parts.
"The elephant of your desire devours the leaves of our wish-creepers; let him be restrained by those who know the Cintāmaṇi jewel of my thoughts, lest he lead us far away!"—
thus do the goddesses of the earth, standing upon the railings of every path, cry out.
While King Siṃha was intent on giving away wish-fulfilling trees, celestial cows, elephants, and other such gifts, [the sage said: SRs_1.313.
I worship the Enemy of Rākṣasas for protection; Vīrabhadra for routing powerful adversaries;
Rāmabhadra for compassion; Rauhiṇeya for ascending the heights of the glory of arm-strength;
Pāñcāla for the art of attending upon fickle-eyed women; and the Full Moon for his graciousness.
King Siṃha, that moon among monarchs, far surpasses even the pride of Kandarpa’s own form.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Delight of the Audience," in the treatise on dramatic ornamentation named *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, composed by King Siṃha, whose strength of arm was terrifying, who was the son of the illustrious Anapotanarendra— the Bhairava unto rival factions and sovereign of the glorious Āndhra region.
May this second chapter, the *Vilāsa*,
which is the delight of connoisseurs,
a mine of auspicious virtues, and a bestower of welfare, be for your benefit.
The splendor whose chest is adorned by the *kāleyaka* paste upon the breasts of Kamalā.
Salutations to her who brings security to both consciousness and matter; to her who is worthy of worship by means of the *śrīparṇaja* and other [medicinal herbs];
to her, the daughter of the ocean, whose lotus rests upon the tip of her hand.

The two prefixes *vi* and *abhi* signify distinction and orientation, respectively; they indicate that [the mental factors] proceed toward the stable [mind] with distinction and orientation. (SRs 2.3)
These transitory states (vyabhicārin) are to be known by their indications through speech, limbs, and disposition;
they also cause that [permanent state] to move toward the course of emotion (bhāva). (SRs 2.4)
Emerging and submerging in the enduring ocean of nectar,
they cause it to swell like waves and attain its very same nature.
Despair, despondency, wretchedness, exhaustion, fatigue, intoxication, pride, apprehension, terror, agitation, insanity, epilepsy, and likewise disease; //SRs_2.6//
Delusion, death, laziness, dullness, shame, and dissimulation; memory, as well as reasoning, reflection, intelligence, and fortitude; joy and longing; //SRs_2.7//
Fury, envy, malice, restlessness, sleep,
slumber, and awakening— these are declared to be the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*).
And from the knowledge of reality, there arises a sense of detachment and self-reproach toward misfortune, calamity, separation, envy, and the like. [SRs 2.9]

But that remorse which arises from the failure to complete an undertaking already begun, from the non-attainment of what was desired, from misfortune, or from the recognition of one's own fault; //SRs_2.10//
That despondency is threefold, based on whether it is superior, middling, or inferior;
seeking companions, means, and reflection are considered [the primary factors] in the superior type. (SRs 2.11)
Lack of enthusiasm, despondency, and so forth are considered the secondary effects (*anubhāva*) of the middling [hero]; for the lowest [hero], they would be despondency and looking about. (SRs 2.12)
Weeping, sighing, meditating, parchedness of the mouth, and so forth,
as well as heartburn, wretchedness, and the like— this state of dejection, characterized by a lack of arrogance, is indeed *dīnatā* (depression).
In that regard, the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) are considered to be the discoloration of the body, rigidity of the limbs, and so forth,
resulting from mental anguish, disease, old age, thirst, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and the like.

In this state, there is a loss of vitality and exhaustion, characterized by emaciated limbs, impaired speech and movement, trembling, lack of energy, discoloration, and the rolling of the eyes. (SRs 2.15)
Fatigue is mental exhaustion caused by traveling, dancing, sexual pleasure, and the like;
it is characterized by the rubbing of limbs, sighing, and likewise the massaging of the feet. (SRs 2.16)
Yawning, languid movement, the rolling of the eyes and mouth,
and the sound of sighing— these are to be known as the consequent states (anubhāvas) arising from fatigue.
Intoxication (*mada*), however, is a confusion caused by the agitation of bliss produced by liquor;
it is threefold, distinguished as mild, moderate, and intense. (SRs 2.18)
In the youthful stage of intoxication, there is a smiling gaze, a flush upon the face, speech agitated by smiles, and graceful, playful movements of the body. (SRs 2.19)
In the moderate stage of intoxication, there is stumbling in speech, rolling of the eyes,
a crookedness in gait, and the tossing or drooping of the arms.

When [the poison] has been drawn out, however, the following symptoms are considered to occur: impairment of movement, loss of consciousness, frequent spitting, labored breathing, hiccups, vomiting, and so forth. (SRs 2.21)
A youth [is appropriate] for those of the highest class and so forth; one of middle age for those of middle and low classes;
and an inferior one for the low classes, in order to increase their respective pride. (SRs 2.22)
One of superior nature sleeps; one of middling nature laughs and sings; one of inferior nature speaks vulgarly and harshly, and weeps. (SRs 2.23)
Some maintain that pride (*māna*) produced by sovereignty and other such factors is called intoxication (*mada*);
however, we remain indifferent [to this], for it is merely a variety of the arrogance (*garva*) that will be described below.
Arrogance is said to be the contempt for others based on one's own sovereignty, beauty, youth, lineage, learning, strength, or the attainment of desired objects and the like. (SRs 2.25)

In this context, there are consequences such as transgressing the command of the guru and other authorities, withholding the unsurpassed [teaching], and even turning away when it is being spoken. (SRs 2.26)
Confusion, concealment, harshness of speech, lack of attention, gazing at one's own limbs, and even the contraction of the body; SRs 2.27.
Suspicion is considered to be the imagining of one's own misfortune due to such things as the crime of theft;
its physical manifestations include frequent glancing at the side and the parching of the mouth. (SR 2.28)
Furthermore, symptoms such as covering the body, discoloration, and a hoarse throat also occur;
this doubt is twofold, distinguished as being either self-originated or caused by another.
This [suggestion] is generally produced by one's own actions and arises from oneself; it is manifested through gestures (*iṅgita*).
Gestures, however, consist of the movements of the eyelashes, the eyebrows, the pupils, and the gaze. (SRs 2.30)
But the arousal of another toward oneself may arise from the improper conduct of that other;
one should generally discern this [arousal] by means of facial expression and gesture. (SRs 2.31)
Manner refers to sattvic activity, while gesture consists of actions arising from the major and minor limbs;
fear, however, is the agitation of the mind caused by lightning, carnivorous beasts, and thunder.

Likewise, the transformations produced therein by spirits, serpents, and the like should be understood as trembling of the limbs, contraction, horripilation, paralysis, and faltering speech. (SRs 2.33)
The agitation of the mind that arises from the confusion of momentary blinking, or from leaning against something nearby, and so forth— this is *āvega* (distress), and it is eightfold.
From seeing portents, windstorms, rain, fire, or intoxicated elephants;
from hearing what is pleasant or unpleasant; and even from the misfortune of enemies.
In that context, portents include earthquakes and the like, as well as the rising of comets and other such signs;
those arising from them consist of the collapsing of all limbs, aversion, and fleeing.
Furthermore, there are such transformations as despondency, paleness of face, and astonishment;
as well as arriving in haste, seizing a garment, and veiling oneself.

The cleansing of the eyes and other such actions arising from a surge of wind, the holding of an umbrella, the contraction of the limbs, and the running with arms crossed in the svastika posture; SRs_2.38.
Seeking warmth and so forth are the activities arising from the onset of rain;
fanning and shaking the limbs are the movements arising from the onset of fire. (SRs 2.39)
There are the tossing about of limbs, the casting of glances, the contraction of the eyes, and so forth;
and when there is agitation produced by an elephant, there is a swift retreat.

Repeated glances toward the rear, along with fear, trembling, and so forth, are considered [the signs] in this state born from hearing news of a beloved; indeed, rising up and embracing [are also included].
In this [state], even when hearing what is unpleasant, there is the giving of gifts, kind speech, horripilation and so forth, as well as lamentation and change of posture. (SRs 2.42)
Crying out, falling down, wandering about, and so forth are the movements that occur during the onset of an enemy; likewise, there is the taking up of armor, weapons, and the like.
Mounting chariots, horses, and elephants, and sudden departures— these are the majestic powers (anubhāvas) of the superior and other types of characters, as appropriate.
Insanity is a derangement of the mind caused by separation or the loss of what is beloved;
however, when born of separation, its activities consist of running about and lamentation.
Incoherent prattle, sleeping, rising suddenly, conversing with inanimate objects, and smiling without cause; SRs 2.46.
But when this [body] has caused the destruction of what is desired, there is the smearing with ashes and the like,
the performance of dance and song, and the wearing of grass and discarded flower garlands.
The aforementioned transformations, such as the wearing of robes and so forth, may also be produced by the defect of an imbalance of the elements or by possession by spirits and the like. (SRs 2.48)
Apasmāra, however, is a disturbance of the mind; its symptoms therein are trembling, running, falling, stiffness, whirling, and distortions of the eyes. (SRs 2.49)

Furthermore, even such things as biting one's own lips, clapping the arms, and foaming at the mouth with saliva are indeed diseases arising from the imbalance of the humors; thus we remain indifferent [to them].
In this case, however, disease may arise from the aggravation of the humors, their depletion, and so forth;
its symptoms include stiffness of the limbs, looseness of the body parts, moaning, and the contraction of the mouth.
The physical transformations such as drooping of the limbs, rolling of the eyes, and labored breathing, accompanied by either coldness or burning heat, are proclaimed to be of two kinds. (2.52)
Moving the jaw, shedding tears, trembling of all the limbs, moaning, contracting the knees, horripilation, dryness of the mouth, and so forth. (SRs 2.53)
In the case of burning fever (dāha-jvara), the symptoms include a desire for cold objects, garlands, and the like,
as well as the tossing of hands and feet, dryness of the mouth, and so forth.
Delusion (moha) is the mind's state of bewilderment caused by calamities, fear, separation, and the like;
its transformations should be understood as the emptiness of the sense faculties. (SRs 2.55)
Lack of movement, the whirling of the limbs, falling, dizziness, and so forth—these result from the separation of the wind known as Dhanañjaya from the self. (SRs 2.56)
Death is that which occurs through the limitation of the body;
and this is said to be of two kinds: born of disease and born of injury. (SRs 2.57)
The first type, however, arises from incurable heart-disease, cholera, and the like;
its symptoms therein include the utterance of indistinct syllables.

Discoloration of the limbs, shallow breathing and so forth, stiffness and closing of the eyes, hiccups, looking toward one's attendants, and the lack of movement in the sense organs [are the signs]. (SRs 2.59)
The second [type of suffering] arises from being struck, falling, milking, being bound, poison, and so forth;
among these, in the case of that arising from being struck and the like, there are falling to the ground, crying out, and so on. (SRs 2.60)
Poison, such as *vatsanābha* and others, has eight stages arising from it:
blackness of the body, trembling, burning sensation, hiccup, frothing at the mouth, and breaking of the neck.

Inertness and death are said to be the first and subsequent [stages] respectively; these are the movements born of impulse, arising from natural state, fatigue, satiety, being full with the fetus, and so forth.
In this context, *ālasya* (laziness) is that state of being disinclined toward action due to exhaustion;
it consists of stretching the limbs, aversion to activity, yawning, and rubbing the eyes. (SRs 2.63)

A fondness for beds and seats, as well as drowsiness, sleep, and so forth, and a dullness consisting of a lack of comprehension upon hearing about desired and undesired objects, constitute [the fault of] *tamas*. (SRs 2.64)
Furthermore, there is the absence of sight, and therein actions such as the lack of blinking, lack of hearing, lack of dependence on others, silence, and so forth. (SRs 2.65)
Modesty consists in not being overly bold due to performing improper acts, contempt, praise, new unions, the failure to retaliate, and so forth. (SR 2.66)
In that state, there is concealed speech, downcast eyes, and reflection;
no departure anywhere outside, and veiling oneself from afar.
Cutting the nails, scratching the ground, and so forth—
these are ways of concealing one's true intentions through the power of deceitful conduct and strategic policy.
Speaking otherwise due to shame, timidity, courtesy, boldness, defeat, and so forth; feigning false fortitude; and looking elsewhere [are forms of deception]. (SRs 2.69)

In this [state], there also arise these attendant manifestations (anubhāvas), such as the breaking off of conversation, brought about by factors like composure, reflection, firm practice, and looking at similar objects. (2.70)
Memory is the cognition of an object previously experienced; therein, the modifications include trembling and lifting of the head, as well as the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth.
Reasoning (*ūha*) is discursive thought (*vitarka*) produced by doubt, deliberation, cognition, and so forth;
it culminates in a conclusion and may be either false or indeed true. (SRs 2.72)

In that regard, the consequential expressions (anubhāvas) would be these: the knitting of the eyebrows, the shaking of the head, and so forth, [arising] from the failure to obtain a desired object, the loss of sovereignty, and the like.
In that [state] consisting of reflection (cintā), which is the nature of meditative absorption (dhyāna), these experiences arise:
emaciation, downward-looking of the face, burning heat, sighing, gasping, and so forth.
Intellect (*mati*) is the determination of meaning resulting from the churning of the chariots of various scriptures;
its activities therein consist of performing what is to be done and the cutting away of doubt. (SRs 2.75)

The casting of eyebrows as instruction for disciples, as well as reasoning and refutation, and so forth, [are accomplished] through the various attainments of knowledge, discernment, devotion to the guru and others, and manifold purposes. //SRs_2.76//
Through shame and other such qualities, the mind’s lack of craving is called fortitude (*dhṛti*).
In this regard, its manifestations (*anubhāva*) are to be known as the experience of having attained one's goals. (SRs 2.77)

Agitation and the like regarding objects that have not been attained, those that are past, or those that have perished, as well as [agitation] through the attainment of a desired object or the success of a suitable undertaking; //SRs_2.78//

Joy (*harṣa*) is the clarity of mind conceived through the company of friends, the grace of gods and others, and so forth; in this context, it is characterized by the blossoming of the eyes and the face. (SRs 2.79)
Affectionate speech, embracing, the emergence of horripilation,
the breaking out of perspiration, and the pressing of hand against hand, and so forth.
Impatience with time is longing arising from separation from a desired object;
its activities include the desire to see that object or other beautiful things, and so forth. (SRs 2.81)
Hastiness, lack of stability, lying down, remaining in a supine position while thinking,
heaviness of the body, sleep, drowsiness, sighing, and so forth.
Cruelty (*caṇḍatva*) and ferocity (*ugratā*) consist of [acts] such as pursuing those who have committed offenses, seizing thieves, and engaging in false speech and the like. (SRs 2.83)
In that regard, his actions consist of redness of the eyes, binding and beating,
shaking the head, and such acts as showing distress, striking, and reviling.
Anger arising from insults, contempt, and the like is called *amarṣa* (impatience). In that state, there is perspiration, shaking of the head, downward gaze, and brooding. (SRs 2.85)
The activities of seeking means, enthusiasm, and perseverance [are undertaken] for the sake of another's good fortune, prosperity, knowledge, valor, and so forth. (SRs 2.86)
The attribution of faults even where virtues exist is envy; therein the physical transformations include turning away the face, reproach, knitting the brows, and showing disregard.
Through passion, hatred, and the like, there arises lightness and fickleness of mind; therein, due to a lack of discernment, one engages in activities such as embracing and clinging.
Harsh speech such as ordering someone to be expelled, as well as striking others and so forth,
arise from intoxication, one's own nature, physical exertion, thoughtlessness, fatigue, and the like.
Sleep is the closing of the mind; its symptoms therein are heaviness of the face, rolling of the eyes, and a massaging or relaxing of the limbs. (SRs 2.90)
Labored inhalation and exhalation, drooping of the limbs, closing of the eyes, contraction of the body, and mental dullness—these and others [are the symptoms]. (SRs 2.91)
An excess of sleep itself constitutes somnolence; its symptoms therein are the cessation of the sense faculties, the closing of the eyes, and the drooping of the limbs. (SRs 2.92)
Furthermore, there are the states of talking in one's sleep, restlessness, and labored inhalation and exhalation,
as well as [the signs of] dreaming, tactile sensations, sounds, the completion of sleep, and so forth.
Awakening is the attainment of consciousness; its physical signs therein are the rubbing of the eyes, rising from the bed, the stretching out of the arms, and the cracking of the fingers.
Scratching the head, twisting the limbs, and so forth—
these are the sattvic transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) occurring in the highest, lowest, and middle [types of characters].
The mental states, such as agitation, affection, hypocrisy, and envy, are to be described as appropriate through both the determinants (vibhāvas) and the consequents (anubhāvas).
Since they are included within those already mentioned, they have not been shown separately;
for the *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas* are mutually dependent upon one another.
The relationship of cause and effect, however, should generally be understood from common worldly experience;
they are twofold—characterized by independence and dependence—and both are subject to deviation.
Those things that have attained the state of nourishing others are called "dependent" (paratantra);
in the absence of that [dependence], those entities are remembered as being "independent" (svatantra).
These [flaws] would be mere semblances when they proceed from impropriety;
because of their unreality and their unsuitability, impropriety is twofold. (SRs 2.100)
