That which pertains to the insentient is caused by unreality; that which has its locus in low beings, animals, and humans is said to be caused by incapacity. (SRs 2.101)
The four stages of the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) are origination, connection, mixture, and subsidence; among these, origination is the emergence of an emotion. SRs 2.102.
If two entities—whether similar or dissimilar, and produced by distinct causes—meet together, that is proclaimed as *saṃdhi* (juxtaposition). // SRs 2.103 //
The dissolution of an excessively intensified state is called tranquility (śānti), whereas the mutual friction of states is their variegation (śavalatva). (SRs 2.104)
By King Siṃha, whose fame travels through the intermediate quarters of the world,
all such wandering beings have been described along with their manifold elaborations.
Those stable entities which are not obstructed by things either of their own class or of a different class lead others to their own nature, just like the ocean [absorbs] rivers. (SRs 2.106)
And Bharata has described these as love, mirth, energy, wonder, anger, sorrow, disgust, and fear; their characteristics will now be explained to you. (SRs 2.107)
The mutual and enduring desire between two youths is *rati* (love),
arising from nature, application, association, and self-conceit.
In that regard, this transformation [of passion] would occur through internal objects by way of similes;
it is considered to consist of side-long glances, the raising of eyebrows, affectionate speech, and so forth. (SRs 2.109)

But Bhoja describes pleasure as being distinct from sexual union; however, that opinion is not accepted because sexual union is already included within the [other] objects such as sound and so forth. (SRs 2.110)

This [love] consists of the enjoyment of sprout, shoot, bud, blossom, fruit, and full fruition, respectively; it is called affection (preman), pride (māna), endearment (praṇaya), tenderness (sneha), passion (rāga), and deep attachment (anurāga). (SRs 2.111)
That love which is the bond of feeling between a young couple, free from any sense of duality,
and which, through its continuous flow of affection, reaches the very core of the heart by virtue of its independence.
That which expands the crookedness of internal disposition through external and internal services devised by love and pride is called *māna* (pride). (SRs 2.113)
That which binds one with the confidence of affection is called *praṇaya* (love);
it occurs when that confidence has reached its highest degree through such means as mutual glances. (SR 2.114)
That wherein the internal organ flows is called *sneha* (affection);
it is said to be of three kinds, distinguished as intense, moderate, and mild. (SRs 2.115)
When the mental state of a beloved person is unknown due to travel abroad and the like,
that affection which causes distress to others is called mature love.
He who tolerates dependence on the experience of others is mediocre;
he who, when one of the two [parties] is engaged in honor and so forth, acts toward the other [in a contrary manner]. (SRs 2.117)
Neither equanimity nor regard—such affection is called "dull";
even when suffering is excessive in the mind, one is attached to it as if it were pleasure.
That intensity of affection by which one is described as "possessing passion" (rāga) is threefold, distinguished by the types of dyes: safflower, indigo, and madder. (SRs 2.119)
That is to be known as the dye of safflower which colors the mind in an instant;
though appearing exceedingly bright, it perishes in just a moment. (SRs 2.120)
But that which is dyed with indigo, once attached, does not fade nor does it shine;
though attached for only a short time, it does not perish even after a long time. (SRs 2.121)
That which is called the madder-red dye shines exceedingly;
it is passion itself that is revealed through its attainment of the state of being known.

If it is argued that "attachment" (anurāga) is defined as the persistence of the substratum [of passion], others maintain that this is a distinction between joy (prīti) and delight (rati); however, that is not our view. 2.123.
This [state] has non-engagement as its object; it does not differ from joy, because of the transformation in speech, appearance, dress, and action. (SRs 2.124)

Furthermore, due to longing for the positions of others and even through imitation of them, there occurs a transformation of the mind known as laughter; its physical manifestations are described therein. (SRs 2.125)
The modification of vision consists of the trembling of the lips, cheeks, and so forth;
its power, aided by self-restraint and other means, lies in actions that are praiseworthy for their results. (SRs 2.126)

The mental state characterized by haste is enthusiasm; therein lie various transformations, such as the observation of time and other factors, as well as fortitude, the commencement of speech, and so forth. (SRs 2.127)
It is defined as being twofold, by way of the distinction between the innate (*sahaja*) and the non-removable (*anāhārya*);
for it precedes the supramundane categories of reality through the worldly [conventions] and so forth.
That expansion of the mind which is wonder is thus described;
its actions therein include the widening of the eyes, eloquent speech, horripilation, and so forth.
The blazing of the mind caused by killing, contempt, and so forth is called anger (*krodha*).
This is threefold, distinguished as *krodha*, *kopa*, and *roṣa*. (SRs 2.130)
Anger, which culminates in killing, mutilation, and the like, is found among cruel people; whereas resentment, which generally lasts until one's request is granted, is found among heroic people.
For those two, there are four objects of focus: enemies, servants, friends, and those worthy of honor;
[their signs] are repeatedly biting the lips, knitting the eyebrows, and grinding the teeth. (SRs 2.132)
Squeezing the hands, trembling of the limbs, waiting for a weapon, looking at one's own arms, and roaring from the throat—these occur when one is enraged by an enemy. (SRs 2.133)

In the case of anger toward a servant, however, the actions should include threatening, striking the head, rebuking in many ways, and repeatedly staring at him with contemptuous looks and the like. (SRs 2.134)
In anger caused by a friend, there may be physical distortions, tears falling from the corners of the eyes, silence, meditation, immobility, and frequent sighing. (SRs 2.135)
Silence, downcast faces, and averted gazes are also gestures used when one’s superior is angry;
however, when censuring oneself, the gestures are self-reproach and a humble countenance.
In the unsurpassed [stage], there are signs such as perspiration and a faltering voice;
however, in the stage of anger toward an enemy, the actions consist of speech imbued with intense emotion.

The knitting of the brows, perspiration on the forehead, the redness of the sidelong glance, and so forth—these actions arising from anger and the like are [the indicators] for the three types of wrath toward servants and others. (SRs 2.138)
Anger between a man and a woman is mutual, yet when directed toward a woman, it ends with her reassurance;
in this case, the resulting transformations include side-long glances.
Trembling of the lower lip, reddening of the corners of the eyes, sighing, and so forth—
anger directed toward a man is said to manifest in women in these two ways.
The first [type of anger] may have a co-wife as its cause, while the other may have a different cause;
such anger caused by a co-wife is elaborated upon in the context of separation.

But in this case, when [the suffering] is caused by other factors, actions are like those born of human anger; it is produced by such things as the death of a kinsman, misfortune, or the loss of wealth. (SRs 2.142)
Sorrow is a burden of mental affliction; its manifestations therein include discoloration, the shedding of tears, dryness of the mouth, stiffness, sighing, and so forth.
This mature superior person, though highly advanced even through the dominant emotions (vibhāvas) residing in others,
is generally pacified by means of his own established fortitude.
In that regard, gestures consist of describing virtues, weeping in secret, and so forth;
this [deceit] may extend up to death when directed toward oneself or others, but it is considered middling when directed toward both.
In that situation, transformations such as weeping that is not too distinct generally arise from causes inherent within women and low-born persons themselves. (SRs 2.146)
There, the earth was encircled by those resolved upon death;
there were breast-beating, rending, falling down, loud wailing, and so forth.
The contraction of the mind caused by the sight, hearing, and so forth of unpleasant objects—this is the transformation known here as *jugupsā* (disgust). (SRs 2.148)
Covering the nose, hurried gait, contorting the face, shaking all the limbs, contemptuous gestures, and frequent spitting—these and the like [are signs of aversion]. (SRs 2.149)
Pure *ghṛṇā* (disgust) is described as a distinct form among the ten types [of *rasas*] in the *Daśarūpa*;
however, it does not differ from the disgust that arises upon hearing of what is to be abandoned. (SRs 2.150)
Fear, however, arises from spells, or from the sight and hearing of things that are terrible; it is an extreme instability of the mind, which generally occurs in those of low or middling character.
In the case of the best [type of person], however, it may arise from causes that are highly extraordinary;
in such fear, there occurs a change in complexion, rigidity, and trembling of the limbs.
Fleeing, looking back, hiding one's own self, parching of the mouth, crying out, seeking refuge, and so forth. (SRs 2.153)
The other types of fear have been explained by the son of Soḍhala as being born of causes; however, artificial fear directed toward superiors and others is considered unreal and superior. (SRs 2.154)
The two types [of *bhayānaka*] are that arising from a terrifying spectacle and that consisting of the frightening of children and others;
among these, the latter is included within the fear produced by hearing something dreadful. (2.155)

Because it is devised as an indication of [threats from] monks, bears, thieves, and so forth, the first [type of speech], however, does not enter the category of fear in the section on reasoning. (SRs 2.156)

Since a disposition indicated by such acts as standing in a lower position in the presence of a guru and others is indeed *vinaya* (humility), it might likewise be present in a drama (*nāṭaka*). (SRs 2.157)
Through his state of concealment, the quality of fear has departed far away;
therefore, it is certain that fear must arise solely from a cause. (SRs 2.158)

Bhoja has stated that other permanent emotions—namely pride, affection, fortitude, and intelligence—are likewise stable even within the exalted, the amorous, the tranquil, and the noble sentiments. (SRs 2.159)

In that regard, affection (*sneha*) is a variety of passion (*rati*); it is threefold, consisting of desire and its products. Others [the transitory emotions] are not suitable for the status of a permanent state (*sthāyibhāva*), because they lack the capacity for nourishment. (SRs 2.160)
Thus, it should be understood that there are exactly eight permanent emotions (sthāyins) approved by the sages;

That face is the cause of various objects and even of aesthetic flavors (rasas),
while the limbs therein exist in accordance with the commencement of the seed-syllables.
Introduction, elaboration, transition, seduction, application, attainment, resolution, arrangement, and contemplation. (SRs 3.32)
One should apply the twelve [elements] as the means for "unfolding" (udbheda) and "division" (bheda);
the "introduction" (upakṣepa), however, is said by the wise to be the indication of the seed (bīja). 3.33.

The wise declare that the attainment of happiness is called "attainment" (prāpti), while the further planting of the seed is here termed "concentration" (samādhāna). (SRs 3.36)
The wise know that which produces pleasure and pain to be destiny;
the cultivation of virtues and other qualities is the wondrous transformation of the mind through praiseworthy means.
The opening of the seed is proclaimed as its "unfolding" (udbheda);
or rather, it is the stimulation of the seed, or the breaking apart of its compact mass. (SRs 3.38)
They define *karaṇa* as the undertaking of the subject matter at hand, wherein there occurs the revelation of the seed through both the visible and the invisible. (SR 3.39)
That [practice] should be directed toward the *bindu* in accordance with effort;
here, the wise should employ thirteen limbs. (SRs 3.40)

Vilāsa (graceful movement), parisarpa (gliding), vidhuta (shaking off), śama (appeasement), narman (jesting), narmadyuti (the brilliance of jesting), pragamana (advancing), nirodha (obstruction), and paryupāsana (attendance).
Flower, thunderbolt, presentation, and likewise the gathering of colors; as well as playfulness and the purpose of union—this is proclaimed as the range of activity. (SRs 3.42)
The constant recollection of a previously seen seed that has been destroyed by such means as the cutting of its sprout is known as *parisarpa*. (SRs 3.43)
When dissatisfaction arises from the failure to obtain the desired objects of the hero and others, that is indeed considered by the wise to be *vidhuta*.
Alternatively, the rejection of the intensification of attachment is "rejection" (nirākṛti);
the wise who know that call this "tranquility" (śama), which is the pacification of dissatisfaction.
The wise know that speech in which jesting predominates is *narma*;
laughter for the purpose of concealing anger is considered *narmadyuti*.
That, however, which is a progressive discourse consisting of successive statements is called *pragamana*;
where a calamity arises, that is declared to be *nirodha*.
That which is a conciliation of one who is angry is called "service" (paryupāsana); that which is a statement with a specific distinction is designated as "flower" (puṣpa). (SRs 3.48)
That which is direct, harsh speech should be known as the "vajra"; that which is a presentation of a point accompanied by logical arguments is intended [as the "needle"]. (SRs 3.49)
The approach to all castes is called the withdrawal of caste;
it is the repeated seeking of the embryo of the seed, both seen and unseen. (SRs 3.50)

In this case as well, one should arrange the constituent elements (aṅgas) in accordance with the requirements of the dramatic action (ācāpatākā): the "bringing forth of the unreal" (abhūtāharaṇa), the "path" (mārga), the "exemplification of form" (rūpodāharaṇa), and the "sequence" (krama). *Śṛṅgāra-śataka* 3.51.
Saṅgraha, anumāna, toṭaka, adhibala,
udvega, sambhrama, and ākṣepa— these twelve are their characteristics.
Falsehood consists of speech that relies on deceit;
the path is the exposition of the true meaning; and form is speech that creates doubt. (SRs 3.53)
That which is a statement of one's own excellence is considered an *udāharaṇa* (illustration);
or it is the knowledge of another’s disposition, or the sequence, or the connection with the matter being contemplated. (SRs 3.54)
Inclusion (saṅgraha) is proclaimed as the conjunction of conciliation and gifts;
the inference from a mark (liṅga) is said to be the deduction of a matter from its signs. (SRs 3.55)
The wise indeed declare that *saṃrambha* is speech accompanied by vehemence; they call *adhibala* the excessive deception through guile. (SRs 3.56)
Fear arising from enemies, enmity, and the like is called *udvega* (agitation).
Suspicion and terror arising from enemies, tigers, and so forth are *sambhrama* (distress). (SRs 3.57)
They describe "implication" (*ākṣepa*) as the introduction of a seed within the womb, wherein one reflects upon seduction, anger, calamity, and so forth. (SRs 3.58)

The meaning of the seed (bīja), once it has burst forth from the womb, is called *vimarśa* (reflection); the arrangement of its constituent parts (*aṅga*) here is determined by its conformity with the *prakarī* (the secondary incident) and the attainment of the inevitable (*niyatāpti*).
Defamation, then quarreling, fleeing, running away, and power; splendor, attachment, deception, exertion, and obstruction.
Persuasion, agitation, and taking—these are the thirteen [means].
Among them, "refutation" (apavāda) is said to be the proclaiming of faults. (SRs 3.61)
Speech composed of faults is declared to be *sampheṭa* (conflict); the mention of opposition, killing, burning, and so forth is proclaimed as *vidrava* (flight). //SRs_3.62//
The sage Bharata has stated that transgression against the guru is a "flowing" fault;
however, the power to pacify a conflict once it has arisen is considered a virtue.
That which is designated as *dyuti* by the wise consists of threatening and alarming;
the narration of a relevant matter is celebrated as *prasaṅga*. (SRs 3.64)
Others describe *prasaṅga* as the praising of one's teachers; they know it as the act of causing humiliation and so forth for the sake of one's own purpose, or as deception. (SRs 3.65)
"Exertion" (vyavasāya) is said to be the manifestation of one's own capability;
"obstruction" (virodhana) is the expression of opposition among those who are embroiled in mutual conflict. (SRs 3.66)
The indication of a future event as if it were already accomplished is *prarocanā* (persuasion);
self-praise is *vicalana*; the taking up [of the plot] is *ādāna*; and the summary of the action is *kāryasaṅgraha*. (SR 3.67)
That [dramatic juncture] in which the *mukha*, *sandhi*, and other elements, combined with the seed (*bīja*), reach their great purpose, is called the *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion). SRs 3.68.

Junction (sandhi), opposition (virodha), knitting together (grathana), decision (nirṇaya), and consolation (paribhāṣaṇa) along with favor (prasāda); likewise, joy (ānanda), convention (samaya), and composition (kṛti) [are features] in the embrace of speech (bhāṣopagūhana). SRs 3.69.
Now, the prior state, the union, the conclusion, and the eulogy—these they call the components of the denouement; I shall, however, state their definitions.

The "seed" (bīja) is the introduction; "junction" (sandhi) is the seeking of the purpose; "conflict" (virodha) would be the obstacle; "knotting" (grathana) is its dismissal; and "determination" (nirṇaya) is the narration of what has been experienced. //SRs_3.71//
Insult (*paribhāṣā*) is mutual verbal abuse or slander;
they say that being pleased (*prasannatva*) is the favor obtained through service and the like. (SRs 3.72)
The teachers declare that *ānanda* is the attainment of the desired object;
*samaya* is the destruction of suffering; and *kṛti* is the firm stabilization of the goal once it has been attained. (SRs 3.73)

The attainment of pride and so forth, speaking, embracing, and the experience of wonder—these may occur when an effect follows its perceived sequence; however, the state of "prior existence" (pūrvabhāva) is [the cause]. (SRs 3.74)

Upasaṃhāra is the statement that the purpose has been accomplished through the attainment of dharma, artha, and so forth; praśasti would be the benediction consisting of the expression of wishes for all beings, both moving and unmoving, by Bharata. (SRs 3.75)

"The teachers declare that the utility of the subordinate elements (aṅgas) consists in their fruitfulness, which depends upon the sentiment (rasa), the emotional state (bhāva), and the specific dramatic purpose."— SRs 3.76.
Some have stated that there is an optionality regarding certain of these constituent parts;
this sequence of the parts at the junctions of the mouth and so forth is not intended to be fixed.

Since the sequence was not strictly adhered to by the earliest authorities such as Bharata and others— those experts who, in their illustrative examples, have also described [the topics] even in a reversed order.
And the sixty-four [arts] were clearly identified by King Siṃha, who knew the vital points of the sixty-four arts, in his *Bālarāmāyaṇa*. (SRs 3.79)
To ensure that the limbs do not appear slack at the joints of the face and other parts, twenty-one types of internal joints (sandhy-antara) should be employed in their respective places. SRs_3.80 //
Out of agreement with other teachers and because of the arising of wonder,
I shall explain their definitions as well as clear examples.
Conciliation and bribery, sowing dissension and punishment, presence of mind, execution, stumbling over one’s lineage, vigor, intellect, anger, rashness, and fear. (SRs 3.82)
Illusion, conventional reality, delusion, the messenger, the determination of causes, a dream, a painting, and intoxication— these are the twenty-one [similes].
In that regard, conciliation (*sāma*) consists of pleasant speech and the manifestation of one's own devotion;
generosity (*dāna*) is the offering of oneself as a substitute, such as by presenting ornaments and other gifts. (SRs 3.84)
Sowing dissension, however, is the inciting of division among friends through deceitful speech;
while punishment consists of threatening those who are undisciplined by means of sight or hearing. (SR 3.85)
Immediate intuition is known as present-mindedness (*pratyutpanna-mati*);
however, the killing of an assassin (*ātatāyin*) would constitute an act of hostility toward life.
That which is a slip regarding one's lineage (*gotra*) is the speaking of a name incorrectly;
whereas *ojas* is the presentation of speech that reveals one's own power. (SRs 3.87)
Thought that culminates in the accomplishment of a desired object is called *dhī* (intellect);
whereas *krodha* (anger) is the inflaming of the mind upon perceiving an offense or the like.
An undertaking devoid of regard for one's own life would be recklessness;
fear is sudden terror; and illusion is the fabrication of deceit. (SRs 3.89)
Concealment (*saṃvṛtti*) is the hiding by oneself of what one has said oneself;
it is an error, a cognition of inversion, because there is no certainty regarding the consequence (*prasaṅga*).
But in the case of a task that is difficult to accomplish, the role of a messenger is to act as an auxiliary;
the ascertainment of the purpose by means of a reason is considered the "ascertainment of the cause" (hetv-avadhāraṇa).
A dream occurring during sleep is considered a verbal disclosure of a secret;
a letter composed with the intended meaning is called a written disclosure. (SRs 3.92)
Intoxication, however, arises from liquor; it produces a wonderful, variegated, and distracting state by distributing its parts through the joints of the limbs, beginning with the face.
In that very context, the conceptualization should be applied individually according to its fixed nature;
however, the application of the intermediate junctures (*sandhy-antara*) is to be understood as being without division.
Likewise, because these [figures] are observed in the junctures (sandhis) without fixed necessity,
they have been described in the *Daśarūpaka* without further analysis.
In my view, the *saṃdhis* (transitions) are not included among the *aṅgas* (constituent parts);
rather, [the drama] is adorned with the qualities of the *saṃdhis* and so forth by one skilled in the means (*upāya*) such as conciliation (*sāma*). (SRs 3.96)
The examination of the intermediate junctures has been fully accomplished by King Siṃha;
thus, through the primary and secondary limbs, it is well-integrated with the splendor of dramatic form.
Your body should clearly be adorned with the thirty-six ornaments;
these consist of the collection of letters that form the ornaments, the cause, the attainment, and the illustration. (SRs 3.98)
Beauty, doubt, illustration, intention, example, proof, renown, courtesy, presumption, and qualification; SRs 3.99.
The accumulation of words is *tulyatarka*; deliberation is its opposite (*tadviparyaya*);
excellence is the transgression of qualities (*guṇātipāta*); and etymological explanation is the praising of qualities (*guṇakīrtana*). (SRs 3.100)
Censure and conciliation, downfall, a fragment, agitation, and longing;
accomplishment without mention, similarity, a garland, and sweet speech. (3.101)
Ask indeed about the thirty-six ornaments that have been taught and observed;
for speech abounding in virtues and figures of speech is considered an ornament. (SRs 3.102)
A sentence is a collection of syllables with distinct meanings and euphonically combined phonemes; it is designated as a "reason" (hetu) when it establishes the matter to be proven. 3.103.
From the thorough knowledge of one part comes the attainment of the remainder;
that sentence whose meaning is hidden yet equivalent [to the intended] is considered an *udāharaṇa*. (SRs 3.104)
The mutual manifestation of one's own nature between a young man and woman is called *śobhā* (beauty).
That speech which ends in uncertainty is declared to be *saṃśaya* (doubt). //SRs_3.105//
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is the presentation of a reason within one's own position for the sake of establishing the probandum;
however, a poetic conceit (abhiprāya) is an imagined mental image based on a resemblance that does not correspond to reality. (SRs 3.106)
Others say that "intention" (abhiprāya) refers to the sense of "mine-ness" regarding an object held dear;
thus, there is a formal enumeration of well-known terms according to their actual meanings. (SRs 3.107)
That illustration is stated for the purpose of excluding indifference toward others: "Accidental attainment" refers to the realization of a desired object occurring unexpectedly. (SRs 3.108)
The accomplishment of a purpose through sentences renowned in the world,
wherein there is compliance with the mind [of others], is declared to be *dākṣiṇya* (courtesy).
When another meaning is inferred because the stated meaning is untenable, that is illustrated as *arthāpatti* (presumption), which is joined with the sweetness of the expression. (SRs 3.110)
Having stated many established primary meanings, that word which is employed where a statement endowed with distinction occurs should be understood as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). (SRs 3.111)
When many words have been employed, that accumulation of many words which possesses a similar meaning should be understood as *padoccaya* (accumulation of words). // SRs 3.112 //
When employed with metaphors or similes that convey a comparable meaning,
the contact with an object not present to the senses is called "analogical reasoning" (tulyatarka).
Investigation (*vicāra*), however, is the description of many means for achieving a single goal;
its opposite, the inversion of investigation (*vicāraviparyaya*), should be understood as the contrary of this. (SRs 3.114)
The successful cultivation [of the subject] is considered [the first type].
"Transgression of qualities" (*guṇātipāta*) is exemplified as the description of qualities in reverse order, after having first proclaimed many qualities and their general supports. (SRs 3.115)
Where a distinction is proclaimed, that should be understood by the wise as an excellence (*atiśaya*);
etymological explanation (*nirukti*) is faultless expression, and names are for the purpose of establishing the meaning. (SRs 3.116)
When even a single person among many who possess extraordinary qualities in the world is addressed by their names, that should be understood as "the praise of qualities" (guṇakīrtana). (SRs 3.117)
Where, while proclaiming faults, one demonstrates a quality through its implication, or while proclaiming qualities, one reveals a fault—that indeed is censure (*garhaṇā*). (SRs 3.118)
Speech primarily consisting of entreaty should be understood by the wise as *anunaya* (conciliation);
falling away from the intended subject to another is declared to be *bhraṃśa* (deviation). SRs 3.119.
A *leśa* (hint) is speech possessing a qualification that brings about the knowledge of an intention;
whereas *kṣobha* (agitation) is the imagining of an effect in one thing when the cause resides in another. (SRs 3.120)
*Manoratha*, however, is the communication of what one intends to say by means of a pretext;
it is indeed the *prastāvanā* (introduction), wherein the remaining meaning is understood even though it is not explicitly stated. (SRs 3.121)
The sage Bharata said that this [beauty] may be established even when not explicitly stated:
"It arises from the description of objects seen, heard, or experienced," and so forth. (SRs 3.122)
Where resemblance is determined through a state of agitation, that is defined as *sārūpya*;
it is described by the wise for the purpose of accomplishing a desired object. (SR 3.123)
It is called a "garland" because it serves many purposes:
that by which one attains similarity [to the Buddha] through clarity, and wherein words are honored. (SRs 3.124)
The manifestation of praise is known as sweet speech;
where an answer is given by means of a question itself, that is celebrated as *pṛcchā* (the interrogative).

But that statement which is uttered after having grasped the meaning of the treatise, which captivates the minds of the wise and has a happy conclusion, is called "instruction" (upadiṣṭa). (SRs 3.126)
That which is described according to its location, its time, and its form—whether it be perceptible or imperceptible—is considered "seen" by one who has seen it. (SRs 3.127)

[*4] Nāṭ 16.169: When the entire remaining meaning is understood through the mere introduction alone, such that it is established even without being explicitly stated, that is proclaimed as *anuktasiddhi* (establishment of the unstated).
Indeed, thirty-six ornaments have been described by the illustrious King Siṃha, who bestowed many ornaments upon the lords of poets.
According to the opinion of the Sage, these are characterized by their defining marks.

Because it is generally endowed with the Dharma through direct instruction, and because it is the locus of all aesthetic sentiments (rasas) perfected through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements; SRs 3.129.
Because it is connected with the perfection of the *prakṛti*, *avasthā*, *saṃdhi*, and so forth, the wise say that the *nāṭaka* is the *prakṛti* of the *prakaraṇa* and other forms. (SR 3.130)
Because they subsist upon the dramatic elements obtained through the force of extension (*atideśa*),
other types of drama (*rūpaka*) are considered modifications (*vikāra*) in relation to the *nāṭaka*.
Therefore, the definition of the drama is stated first:
it must be endowed with either a divine or a human hero who is steadfast and noble (dhīrodātta). SRs 3.132.
It should be based on either the erotic or the heroic sentiment as its predominant rasa,
connected with a well-known narrative, and endowed with five junctures (sandhis).

[It is characterized] by the fundamental states (*prakṛti*), the junctures (*avasthā*), the limbs of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*), the intervals between junctures (*sandhyantara*), the ornaments (*vibhūṣaṇa*), the flags (*patākā*), the fixed positions (*sthānaka*), the modes of action (*vṛtti*) along with their sub-divisions, and the activities (*pravṛtti*). // SRs 3.134 //
A drama (*nāṭaka*) endowed with the *viṣkambhaka* and other elements bestows the three aims of human life;
therefore, I shall now describe this method for commencing a drama. (3.135)
Just as the intention of the author becomes the very mouth [of the work], so too is the *prastāvanā* (prologue) considered to be the mouth of the principal composition. (SRs 3.136)

The introduction (*prastāvanā*) is said to be the means for establishing the subject matter to be presented; at the beginning of the introduction, however, an auspicious *nāndī* should be performed. (SRs 3.137)
It is traditionally held that [a work] should begin with one of these three: a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter;
it is generally marked by the name of the author and resplendent with words of auspicious meaning. (SRs 3.138)
Others have declared that this *iṣṭā* meter may be employed with eight, ten, or twelve feet, whether they be equal or unequal.
At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the wise *sūtradhāra*, having entered the stage,
should indeed employ the *bhāratī* style of speech for the purpose of preparing the performance.
And its four constituent parts were described by Bharata as *prarocanā*, *mukha*, *vīthī*, and *prahasana*. (SR 3.141)

The *vīthī* and the *prahasana* will be explained clearly in their respective contexts; however, that which is proclaimed by means of praising the subject matter at hand is called *prarocanā*. (SRs 3.142)
And that which brings about the manifestation of the mental fluctuations of the members [of the assembly]—praise should be known as twofold, based on the sentient and the insentient. (SRs 3.143)
Place and time are insentient; time is the beginning of spring and autumn, while place is said to be a sacred site, a royal residence, a pilgrimage center, and so forth.

Therefore, let it be observed that in such expressions as "today is the festival of the Lord of Time," the conscious elements are considered to be the narrator, the poet, the members of the assembly, and the actors.
The lords of stories, however, are those conducive to the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
among them, Yudhiṣṭhira, Nala, and others are those conducive to dharma.
Rudra, Narasiṃha, Nṛpa, and others are examples of those who employ *artha* (plot);
Vidyādhara, the Lord of Vatsa, and others are examples of those who employ *rasa* (sentiment). //SRs_3.147//
Rāma, Vāsudeva, and others are considered to be means for liberation;
however, some maintain there is no distinction between the means for religious duty (*dharma*) and the means for liberation (*mokṣa*).
But poets are the authors of compositions; they may be of four kinds, according to the distinction of being noble, haughty, mature, or humble. (SRs 3.149)
The expression of pride that is hidden within is called *udātta* (the noble);
however, one who speaks of his own excellence through the disparagement of others is said to be *uddhata* (the arrogant).
One who asserts his own excellence as is appropriate is called "prauḍha" (mature);
by others, one who asserts his own excellence through reasoning is remembered as "prauḍha. (SRs 3.151)
One who is disciplined through excellence in discipline reveals his own inferiority;
however, those people who are free from the desire for spectacle should be known by the wise as true members of the assembly.
They too are clearly twofold: those who are to be requested and those who request;
[the latter say], "I shall employ this; please grant me your permission. (SRs 3.153)
They are to be entreated by the stage director; they are known as those who should be requested, their hearts filled with longing, saying, "May the performance be carried out by you. (SRs 3.154)
Those who seek out the reciters of the Sūtras are known as the *prārthakas* (petitioners) among the members of the assembly;
those who subsist on the stage are called actors (*naṭas*), and they too are remembered as being of three kinds.
According to the learned, there are debaters, singers, and dancers;
those who play instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*veṇu*), and drum (*mṛdaṅga*) are known as instrumentalists (*vādaka*). (SRs 3.156)
Those who sing the *dhruvā* verses during the dialogue are considered *gāyakas*;
those who perform various types of dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) are known as *nartakas*. //SRs_3.157//
One should employ an introductory appeal either in detail or in brief;
having thus won over the members of the assembly, the author of the aphorisms should then compose the *āmukha*.

When the Sūtradhāra speaks to the Naṭī regarding his own business through skillful means, using striking speech that alludes to the subject at hand, that is called the *āmukha* (prologue). (SRs 3.159)

Three factors of the introduction are stated: the introductory narrative (*kathodghāta*), the instigator (*pravartaka*), and the excellence of application (*prayogātiśaya*); their definitions are now stated. (SRs 3.160)

When an actor enters by adopting either the words or the meaning of a sūtradhāra’s speech as being consistent with his own past history, it is considered a *kathodghāta* (the introduction of the story), which is of two kinds.
The "instigator" (pravartaka) would be that which, by its temporal equivalence, initiates [the action];
this occurs through the stage-manager's performance, by way of the introductory remark, "This is he. (SRs 3.162)
That which indicates the *prayoga* (the performance) is indeed the *prayogātiśaya*;
this *āmukha* (prologue) is twofold: the *prastāvanā* (introduction) and the *sthāpanā* (establishment). (SRs 3.163)
The Sūtradhāra engages in dialogue with the Vidūṣaka, the Naṭī, and the Pāripārśvika; these are the elements of the *āmukha*, accompanied by a few elements of the *vīthī*. (SRs 3.164)
That which is employed by those learned in drama is known as the *prastāvanā* (prologue),
consisting of extensive passages joined with all the limbs of the *āmukha*, the limbs of the *vīthī*, and other elements.
When the Sūtradhāra converses with the Naṭī, the Vidūṣaka, the Naṭa, and others, and thereby introduces the subject matter at hand, that is indeed the Sthāpanā.
The sequence of the prologue (āmukha) is suitable for a drama abounding in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), such as the *Ratnāvalī* and others; let this be observed primarily by the learned. (3.167)
In plays characterized primarily by heroism, marvels, and the like, the *prastāvanā* (prologue) is generally appropriate;
let this be observed for the most part in works such as the *Anargharāghava*.
However, in cases where the predominant [sentiments] are the comic, the loathsome, the furious, and so forth, the establishment [of the rasa] is considered to be through the *sthāpanā* (fixing);
let that generally be observed in instances such as the unfolding of Vīrabhadra. (SRs 3.169)
The components of the *āmukha* (prologue) have been explained; now we shall describe the components of the *vīthī* (theatrical performance).
It is agreed that these are common to both the *āmukha* and the *vīthī*.
The expansion of their dramatic elements within the performance is due to their necessity in the acting;
these include the *udghātyaka*, *avalagita*, *prapañca*, *trigata*, and *chala*. (SRs 3.171)

In the *vākkeli* and *adhibala* [meters], there are thirteen [syllables] in the *gaṇḍa*, *avasyandita*, and *nālika* [varieties], including *asatpralāpa* and *vyāhāra*, and they are soft (*mṛdu*). (SRs 3.172)
Among those, the *udghātyaka* consists of a series of mutual conversations; it is indeed of two kinds:
by way of the sequence of words with hidden meanings and synonyms, and by way of the sequence of questions and answers. (SRs 3.173)

The "double-sided approach" (dvidhāvalagita) is said to consist of two types: that which consists of an indirect approach toward a goal, and the successful accomplishment of one matter through the context of another. (SRs 3.174)
But mutual praise is mere proliferation (*prapañca*), which is unreal and causes laughter;
because of the similarity of the Vedic texts, the application of multiple meanings may result in a threefold confusion.

Chala (quibble) is said to be [the use of] words that appear affectionate but are accompanied by irony; vilobhana (enticement) is the seduction of one who is full of longing; and vākkeli (verbal play) consists of the completion of a sentence that was left incomplete.

A minister should be addressed as "brāhmaṇa" by other brāhmaṇas, and as "amātya" or "saciva";
a charioteer should address his master as "ārya" or "āyuṣmat."
By the words *tapasvin* and *sādhu*, one who is tranquil is designated;
*svāmī* refers to a crown prince, while *kumāra* and *bhartṛdāraka* refer to a young prince.
*Āvutta* refers to the husband of one’s sister; *pṛtanāpati* means a commander of an army; *bhaṭṭinī*, *svāminī*, *devī*, and likewise *bhaṭṭārikā* denote a mistress or queen.

Attendant women should address royal favorites as "lady" (*yoṣit*), but the chief queen should be addressed by the king as "goddess" (*devī*), while others are to be called "beloved" (*priyā*). (SRs 3.324)
In all cases, however, the wife should be addressed as "Āryā" using her father's name or that of her son;
likewise, a father should be addressed by his son as "Tātapādāḥ," and a mother as "Ambā."
Elder brothers are to be addressed as "Ārya" by their younger siblings; likewise, maternal uncles and others are to be so addressed.
One who is of equal age should be called "Sadṛśa," or addressed by a term of endearment such as "Vayasya."
A female friend should be addressed as "friend" by another friend;
likewise, children, disciples, and juniors should indeed be addressed as such by their elders.
By such designations as "child," "little son," "long-lived one," "dear one," or "born [of us]," one who is younger is addressed by his elders and other people. (SRs 3.328)
One should address those of high status by their craft or their name, or as "Bhadra" or "Bhadrāmukha"; however, for those of low or very low status, one should use "Haṇḍe" or "Hañje" respectively.
Servants should be addressed by their master using their own respective names or by titles appropriate to their craft; in such a manner, the application of designations should be employed.
This should be understood by those skilled in poetry as being consistent with worldly convention and the treatises;
even for a chamberlain or others whose names are not explicitly mentioned, they are to be recognized when they are well-known.

In a fictionalized narrative, however, the poet should clearly invent names for the protagonist and other characters that are appropriate to the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the subject matter (vastu).
The names of chamberlains, such as Vinayandhara, Bābhravya, Jayandhara, and Jaya, should generally indicate their trustworthiness. (SR 3.333)
One should assign names to the maidservants using the names of graceful objects such as creepers, ornaments, and flowers, which have their meanings established through their qualities.
"Karabha," "Kalahamsa," and so forth are the names of the attendants;
"Karpūra," "Caṇḍa," "Kāmpilya," and so forth are the names of the bards. (SR 3.335)
One should assign names such as Subuddhi and Vasubhūti to the ministers; Devarāta and Somarāta are the names for the domestic priests (purohita).
Śrīvatsa, Gautama, Kautsa, Gārgya, Maudgalya,
Vasantaka, and Kāpileya— thus is Vidūṣaka to be named.
With majesty, heroism, victory, pride, valor, and daring—
each word following the previous one adorned like the ornaments, crest-jewels, and garlands of spring.
A wise man should give names to leaders of noble character:
"Candrāpīḍa" (Moon-encircled) and "Kāmapāla" (Protector of Desire), for instance, are names for those of graceful nature.
A wise man should assign names ending in "Datta" or "Senā" for Vaiśyas whose minds are haughty, such as Ugravarmā, Caṇḍasena, and so forth. (SRs 3.340)
The heroine is generally designated by names such as Karpūramañjarī, Candralekhā, Rāgataraṅgikā, or Padmāvatī. (SRs 3.341)
The goddesses, however, were known by names such as Dhāriṇī, Lakṣmī, Vasumatī, and others—
Bhogavatī, Kāntimatī, Kamalā, and Kāmavallarī.
A female practitioner (bhoginī) is known by names such as Irāvatī, Haṃsapadī, and so forth;
whereas those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes have names ending in Śarman, Varman, and Datta, respectively.
The lords of the Vidyādharas are named Śikhaṇḍa, Aṅgada, Cūḍā, and Anta; the Kāpālika people are named Kuṇḍala, Ānanda, Ghaṇṭā, and Anta.
The women of the Kāpālikas are known by such names as Yogasundarī, Vaṃśaprabhā, Vikaṭamudrikā, and Śaṅkhakeyūrikā.
A married woman [should be honored] under such names as Ānandinī, Siddhimatī, Śrīmatī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Yaśovatī, or Putravatī. (SRs 3.346)
Having reflected upon all this, the definition was formulated by the wise poet; thus, the poetry he composed shall shine as long as the moon and sun endure. (SRs 3.347)

Let this treatise be examined with a mind free from envy by those whose intellects have been refined through the knowledge of the characterized, the characteristics, and their manifestation. (SRs 3.348)
The illustrious King Siṃha, a master of the Bharata treatise and a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, has thus composed this *Rasārṇavasudhākara*.
During the mobilization for the expedition of King Anapotasiṃha,
as the sounds of the kettledrums resounded with the repeated cry of "dhaṇam dhaṇam dhaṇam," his veteran warriors rejoiced, shouting "raṇam raṇam raṇam."
The rival kings perceive every blade of grass as "grass, grass, grass. (SR 3.350)

Thinking that the earth was light on the scale, when King Siṃhacandra was created by the Creator, it became exceedingly heavy; yet even as it was filled to its limits with successively placed deposits of heaps of wish-fulfilling gems, rows of kalpa-trees, and circles of fragrant jewels, [it remained light].
Led upward by his power of levitation, that sky is even today still being filled by hundreds of his enemies' clans.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Radiance of Sentiment" (Bhāvakollāsa), in the treatise on dramatic poetics named *Rasārṇavasudhākara*, composed by King Siṃha— who was as formidable as Bhairava to the rival factions of the illustrious Āndhra region, the son of the illustrious King Anapota, and whose own arm-strength was terrifying. //3//
And this *Rasārṇavasudhākara* is completed;
may Hari— who dwells on the mountain of water (the ocean), who is dark as a tamāla tree,
and who is the auspicious autumnal moon to the cakora-birds that are the sages— be victorious!
The vast expanse of his stainless chest was anointed with the beauty of the saffron paste from the clusters of blossoms upon the breasts of Lakṣmī.
The wind dwelling on the Malaya mountain, the moon with its cool rays, and the bodiless Love-god whose virtuous fame is shared by his friends—
these wander for long, remaining unseen even by elephants.
May that five-arrowed one, who is saluted by multitudes of connoisseurs, be victorious!
May the succession of blessings from all those born of the twice-born cause auspiciousness to surge forth, and may the lifespan of poets be long.
